A prompt is the brief that you give Claude: the task and everything that Claude needs to do it. Briefing well is not a technical skill. It is the same skill that you use when you delegate work to a colleague. Every other objective in this certification depends on it. A good brief gives the other six domains something to work with. No feature, model choice or troubleshooting step fixes a bad brief.
This lesson uses one made-up example throughout: a roofing firm. Its office manager wants Claude to draft a one-page update on this month's jobs for the firm's two directors. The one-line version of this prompt is "write something about this month's jobs".

Anthropic's guidance is to treat Claude as a brilliant but new employee. This employee is highly capable and has no context on your company, project or standards until you supply it. The Help Center gives chat users the same comparison: a newly hired contractor who needs very specific instructions. The Help Center also advises that you explain a failing prompt as if to someone with no background knowledge of what you are asking.

An effective prompt contains as much context as possible, because Claude works from what you give it. When you delegate work well, you cover the task, the background, the audience, the format and what a good result looks like. A prompt covers the same things. Neither a new hire at the roofing firm nor Claude knows which jobs ran late.

A complete business prompt has five parts.
Task. Say precisely what you want done, with a verb and a deliverable. "Draft a one-page project update for the steering committee" is a task. "Help me with my project" is not a task. The office manager's task is a one-page update on this month's jobs for the directors.
Context. Give the background that Claude cannot know. That is who the audience is, what the document is for, what has already been decided, and any constraints that apply. For a writing task, the prompt outlines the requirements, the target audience and the main points.

Source material. Paste or attach the actual inputs, such as the report, the meeting notes or the data. Do not describe them from memory. Claude works from what you give it. A summary from memory adds errors and omissions that the real document does not have. claude.ai accepts documents, spreadsheets and images, so you can give Claude the real inputs. The roofing firm attaches its job sheets instead of describing them from memory.
Output specification. Format, length, tone and structure: three bullet points per workstream, neutral tone, under 400 words.

An example, when standards matter. One sample of a previous document in the house style (your organisation's own style rules) works better than three paragraphs that describe the style. Anthropic calls examples one of the most reliable ways to guide format, tone and structure. Last month's update is the roofing firm's sample.

Opening a prompt with a role, such as "As an HR communications specialist", shapes vocabulary, tone and priorities. Anthropic notes that even a single sentence makes a difference.
Naming the audience changes the output more than most small edits to the instructions do. The same analysis should read differently for the board and for the project team. Claude shapes the analysis if you tell it who is reading. So the roofing firm's brief names the directors. When you explain the reason for a requirement, you also get a more targeted response.

A vague prompt produces generic output, and generic output needs a lot of rework. Being specific about the desired output format and constraints improves Claude's results. A minute that you spend on the brief saves a round of rework. The official usage guidance agrees: be specific and concise, and review and edit your prompt before you send it. A first attempt with a good brief costs less time and less usage than correcting the output more than once. The roofing firm's one-line prompt gives no job sheets, readers or format.

"Technical" does not mean code. At this level, it means asking Claude for a spreadsheet formula, a first attempt at simple data analysis, or a technical document's first draft. The skill is the same: brief the task well. The office manager might write: I need a formula that flags any invoice more than 30 days overdue, here is a sample of the data.

The recurring wrong answer in this objective is the one-line prompt, "write something about our Q3 results". That answer presents the prompt as acceptable because Claude will infer what is needed. Claude cannot infer it: the prompt gives Claude none of the five components to work from. The formula brief above covers what Domain 1 tests. The question never tested how elegant the formula is.
[Key Concept] When an exam question compares prompts, count the components. The right answer almost always supplies the missing task, context, source material, output specification or example. The wrong options improve the wording, and the missing component stays missing.

[Exam Trap] Accepting the one-line prompt because Claude will infer what is needed
Claude has none of the context a colleague would need, so the output is generic and the user spends time on rework because the brief was skipped. Briefing the task properly at the start is the documented fix.
[Exam Trap] Choosing the option that improves the wording while the missing component stays missing
Questions that compare prompts usually test a missing component: no audience, no source material, no format. A change to the wording only leaves that gap open. Supplying the missing component is what fixes the output.
[Exam Trap] Writing the deliverable yourself and using Claude only to proofread

It looks like diligence, but it under-uses the tool. Drafting from a good brief is exactly the work Claude does well. A role that only proofreads loses the time saving. The exam treats it as lazy under-use of the tool.

A facilities coordinator needs Claude to draft a staff memo introducing a new desk-booking system to all office-based staff. She has the supplier's how-to guide and wants a draft she can send without reworking it by hand or going back to Claude for more rounds. Which prompt prepares the work best?
Option ASend a single line asking for a memo about the desk-booking system, keeping the request short so Claude has creative freedom, and plan to pick the best parts of whatever comes back
Option BWrite the memo yourself from the how-to guide and ask Claude only to check the spelling, grammar and tone of the finished text before it goes out to staff

Option CAttach the one-page how-to guide, name the audience as all office-based staff, state the goal of cutting confusion in the first week, and ask for a friendly but firm tone, 300 words, with a three-bullet summary at the top
Option DAsk Claude first to describe how desk-booking systems usually work, then let it draft the memo in whatever format it judges best, supplying the guide, the audience and the tone preferences in later follow-up rounds if the first draft turns out to miss them
[Check Answer]

Claude gives its best output on complex work when you split the work into pieces that Claude can do properly, one at a time. That splitting is task decomposition. Connected parts pass results to each other: a later part needs an earlier part's output or decisions. Independent parts work on their own.
A single well-formed prompt handles a lot of work, but it has a limit. When you put a whole project's requests into one message, the result is shallow and uneven. Claude does some parts well and gives other parts little attention.

This lesson uses one made-up example throughout: a supermarket. Its manager writes a quarterly customer-feedback report for head office. The report needs an outline, sections in one voice and an action list. She also needs a rival-store summary, a press release and a budget table. The Help Center's list of remedies for an unhelpful answer includes breaking complex requests into substeps. The Help Center also says that a prompt should contain as much context as possible.

Numbered steps inside one prompt. For connected parts, list them explicitly. The manager writes: first summarise the feedback themes, then rank them by frequency, then draft one improvement action per theme. Claude follows an explicit sequence far more reliably than one long paragraph of requests. Anthropic's guidance is to use numbered sequential steps when order or completeness matters, and to be specific about output format and constraints.

Staged prompting in one conversation. For a deliverable that you build in stages, ask for the outline, review and adjust it, then draft section by section. You review each stage's output before the next stage runs. The approved output becomes the starting point for the next stage. So you correct the work while correcting still takes little effort. The manager corrects her outline before any section exists.
Plan-first prompting. When the right structure is not obvious, ask Claude to propose an approach first. For example: before writing anything, list the sections you would include and what each covers. Reviewing a plan takes seconds. Reworking a wrong 2,000-word draft does not take seconds.

Separate conversations per sub-task. Put genuinely independent pieces, such as a rival-store summary, a press release or a budget table, in separate chats. Separate chats keep each context clean and focused. The manager gives each of her three side jobs its own chat.

Connected parts belong in one conversation, in stages, so that later stages start from the approved earlier stages. Independent deliverables belong in separate chats. When the structure is unclear, ask for the plan first. A mismatch between technique and task fails in one of two ways. The first is one very large prompt that asks for a finished 20-page product in one pass. The second is connected work that you split across chats. Each new chat has then lost the outline and tone decisions that the previous chat made. Report sections that the manager splits across chats would lose her outline and tone.

A new conversation does not automatically contain another conversation's working material. Claude does now remember across chats. This memory is a set of individual topics that cover your role, projects, preferences and ongoing work context. Memory is context about you, not a transcript. Memory does not carry your approved outline, tone guide or half-finished draft into a new chat. On paid plans, you can ask Claude to search past chats and bring relevant details into the current chat. That search is retrieval that you must ask for, not automatic carry-over.

The dependable pattern is explicit persistence: you carry outputs forward yourself. Paste the output into the new conversation, re-attach the file, or keep the output in a Project's knowledge base. Projects are self-contained workspaces with their own chat histories and knowledge. When the manager returns to the report in a new chat, she first pastes her outline into the chat. Carrying outputs forward is your job, not the product's.

The exam tests matching a technique to a situation, not reciting the four. The right answer follows the three matching rules. Both failure modes appear as wrong options. Where persistent material should be stored is a Domain 3 and Domain 5 question.
Current state (September 2026)

Memory became available on claude.ai on 11 September 2025 for Team and Enterprise plans, then for Pro and Max from 23 October 2025. As of 30 September 2026 memory is on by default for Free, Pro and Max. As of that date, on Team and Enterprise an owner decides whether memory is available. Memory stays off for each member until that member enables it. Chat search, which lets you ask Claude to reference past conversations, is available on paid plans. Neither feature changes the rule: memory saves context about you as individual topics, and you must ask for chat search.

[Exam Trap] One very large prompt that asks for everything, chosen to keep the whole deliverable in one place
Attention spreads unevenly across a project of requests in one message. As a result, some sections are strong and others are skimmed. Corrections also arrive only after the whole thing is wrong. Breaking complex requests into substeps is the documented remedy.
[Exam Trap] Fragmenting connected work across separate conversations
Each new chat lacks the outline, tone decisions and approved material that the previous chat built. So the pieces arrive in different voices. They need reconciling by hand. Separate chats are for independent deliverables, not connected ones.

[Exam Trap] Plan-first prompting offered where the structure is already known and agreed
Asking Claude to propose sections you have already settled is a small unnecessary extra step: it adds a review round without adding information. Plan-first is useful only when the right structure is genuinely unclear.

A programme director at a charity must produce a 20-page annual impact report: an overview, five sections drafted from the notes of five different programme teams, and one consistent voice throughout. The director wants to approve each part as it is produced, and never to explain settled decisions again to a new chat. How should the director structure the work with Claude?
Option ASend one prompt with the notes from all five teams and request the complete 20-page report, overview included, in a single pass so nothing is lost between chats and the voice stays consistent

Option BUse one conversation: agree the outline and a tone guide first, then draft section by section, each prompt carrying the notes for that section, with the overview written last from the finished sections
Option CAsk each of the five programme teams to run its own Claude chat in whatever style it prefers, then combine the six resulting drafts into a single document afterwards
Option DOpen six separate conversations, one per section and one for the overview, so each chat stays small and focused and no single conversation reaches its length limit
[Check Answer]

A first output, Claude's first answer to a prompt, is a draft. The prompt that set the task is the brief. Feedback is the follow-up message that you send about the output. Iteration is the cycle of output, specific feedback and better output. Iteration is the normal way of working, not a failure. The Help Center's getting-started advice says this directly: do not hesitate to refine your prompts or ask follow-up questions. People who get the most from Claude plan one or two rounds of feedback for every task. People who get the least accept a mediocre first attempt, or abandon the tool after one attempt.

This lesson uses one made-up example throughout: a dental practice. Its manager asks Claude for a letter that reminds patients that their check-up is due. The draft has the right parts but is too formal, too long and full of clinical terms.

The Help Center names feedback as an official remedy for an unhelpful answer: provide follow-up instructions, clarify, or ask for a rewrite. "Make it better and try again" reproduces the problem, because the message adds no new information to the conversation. Suppose the manager writes "Cut it to 200 words, keep the paragraph on fees, and lose the marketing adjectives." That message fixes the draft, because each clause names a gap.
Good feedback does one of three things:
It adds a missing constraint, such as the audience, the format or the thing to avoid.
It corrects a misreading.
It narrows the scope.

All three depend on diagnosis: find the gap between the output and the need, then state the gap plainly. A quick method is to check the output against the five components of the original brief. The gap is usually where a component was weak or missing. The manager's one-line prompt never named the audience.
Asking for variants is iteration too. The manager can request three versions of the opening paragraph: formal, conversational and urgent. Claude generates the options, and the manager judges them. This method is often the fastest way to find the right register, or style, when you know something is wrong but cannot yet name it.

When the output is close to what you need, refine it. Stay in the conversation and give targeted follow-ups. Sometimes the output shows that the original prompt was wrong: the wrong task, the wrong framing or missing context. Then rewrite the brief and start a new conversation, rather than correct a misunderstanding through six follow-up turns. A long series of corrections makes the context that the conversation keeps less clear. Each correction also works against the original framing instead of fixing it.

The miscall, the wrong choice between refining and re-briefing, happens in both directions. One miscall is to correct, turn after turn, a brief that asked for the wrong thing. The other miscall is to abandon a conversation that one specific fix would have finished. If the manager's letter needs only plainer words, one follow-up finishes it.

h: Three Responses to a Disappointing Draft
t: You can respond in three ways to a draft that is structurally fine but wrong for its purpose. The vague retry, "not quite, try again", produces the same shortfall, because the retry adds nothing new to the conversation. The targeted follow-up names the tone, the phrases to avoid and the reader that the piece is for. The targeted follow-up produces a usable revision, because each named gap shows Claude what to fix in the rewrite. The manager names a warm tone, no clinical terms, and patients as the reader.

h: Three Responses to a Disappointing Draft
t: The third response is the re-brief. Use it when the original one-line prompt was the real problem. An effective prompt contains as much context as possible, and one line holds very little context. Re-brief properly: attach the style guide and name the audience at the start. A proper re-brief fixes the current batch and improves every batch that follows.

Suppose that two rounds of feedback finally produce the right output. Then the feedback that fixed the draft is exactly the instruction that the original prompt was missing. Add that feedback to the original prompt. The reusable prompt then starts the next run from the improved version, rather than from the beginning. The manager's next batch starts from a prompt that names the tone, plain words and the patient audience.

The exam tests the quality of feedback and ranks the three responses. It rewards the targeted follow-up over the vague retry every time. It expects you to recognise when the re-brief is the professional choice. Questions test the miscall in both directions. When a task recurs every week, moving its wording into standing configuration (instructions that stay in place for every run), such as the instructions of a Project, belongs to Domain 5. Domain 1 stops at refining the current request and keeping the wording that worked.
Why start a new conversation?

Longer chats consume more of your usage limit. When a chat approaches its length limit, the documented advice is to start a new conversation or use a Project. Restarting on a wrong brief is recommended as professional working practice, because a long series of corrections gives an unclear starting point. Official documentation does not claim that long conversations degrade output quality.

[Exam Trap] The vague retry that looks like diligence
Regenerating, rewording slightly, or asking Claude to try again adds no new information to the conversation, so the next output repeats the shortfall. Feedback only works when it names the gap: the audience, the tone, the length, the constraint that was missing.
[Exam Trap] Making small fixes to a fundamentally wrong brief through many follow-up turns
When the output shows the original prompt asked for the wrong thing, each correction works against the framing instead of fixing it. Rewriting the brief and starting a new conversation is faster and gives every later batch of the same work a better starting point.

[Exam Trap] Starting a fresh chat when the output needed only one specific fix
This is the miscall in the other direction. A restart discards the context and approved material the conversation already holds; when the output is close, a single targeted follow-up in the same conversation is the cheaper, faster, professional choice.

A retail merchandiser asks Claude for product descriptions for a seasonal homeware catalogue. The first batch is structurally fine but generic and in the wrong voice. The same prompt in a new chat came back just as generic, and she wants the copy fixed in one more round. What is the most effective next prompt?
Option AStart a brand-new chat, paste the same one-line prompt in again, and rely on the fresh conversation to produce a fresher and more distinctive voice for the batch
Option BAccept the copy as a reasonable starting point, then rewrite the voice by hand across all forty descriptions before the catalogue goes to print

Option CReply with specific feedback naming the required tone, the overused phrases to avoid, and the shopper the catalogue is speaking to, then rerun the batch
Option DReply that the copy is not quite right, ask Claude to try again, and keep regenerating in the same conversation until a batch finally arrives in the right voice
[Check Answer]

A task type is the kind of work that you give to Claude. This objective covers four task types. They are analysis (finding what material shows), research (gathering from sources), drafting (writing a piece) and brainstorming (generating ideas). Anthropic's documentation shows Claude doing all four. Claude analyses chart data, drafts anything from a text message to a screenplay, and generates viewpoints and recommendations as an ideas partner. One prompting style does not fit all four. Each type gets the best results from a different briefing shape. The briefing shape is what the prompt contains.

This lesson uses one made-up example throughout: a lettings agency. Its manager has four jobs this month. She must learn why tenancy renewals fell and compare other agencies' tenant screening. She must also write to landlords about a new fee and find ways to win more landlords.

Analysis starts with the material. Attach the spreadsheet or paste the survey results, because Claude works from what you give it. Uploads give Claude the real artefacts, even documents that are hundreds of pages long.
Then name the questions that the analysis must answer and the decision that the analysis will inform. "Analyse this data" gives Claude no target, so Claude describes the data rather than analyses it. The manager attaches her renewals spreadsheet and asks why renewals fell, which properties lost most tenants, and what should change before next year. Ask for main findings, supporting evidence and caveats. Also ask how Claude reached each conclusion, so that you can check the reasoning. Checking that reasoning is Domain 2 work.

h: Research: A Scoped Question, Not a Topic
t: For multi-source questions, Research works agentically: Claude runs multiple searches, and each search uses the results of earlier searches. Claude then returns a report with citations that are easy to check. For a quick current fact, an ordinary web search suffices. The documentation separates the two in this way: web search suits straightforward factual queries that one or two searches answer. Research suits thorough gathering across many searches.

h: Research: A Scoped Question, Not a Topic
t: Either way, brief a research question, not a topic. State the scope, the angle, and what the findings must inform. The manager asks Research how agencies of her size locally screen tenants, so that she can decide whether to change her own screening. A bare topic gives the searches no direction, and Claude returns an unfocused report. Then verify the citations that matter.

Drafting needs the full five-component brief from objective 1.1: audience, purpose, tone, length and format. Add an example when house style matters, because an example is one of the most reliable ways to guide format, tone and structure. For the fee letter, the manager names landlords as the audience and attaches a past letter. Expect to iterate (objective 1.3). For any long piece, stage the work (objective 1.2): outline first, then sections.

Brainstorming reverses the drafting approach. First, ask for many different ideas: quantity and range, such as twenty ideas that include some unconventional ones. To get ideas beyond the obvious ones, ask for them explicitly, rather than leaving Claude to infer that you want them. Withhold judgement, because heavy constraints reduce the variety, and variety is the purpose of this step. Then narrow the ideas in a second step: apply your criteria, make a shortlist, and develop the ideas that remain. The manager asks for twenty ways to win landlords and applies her budget limit only at the shortlist step. This two-step method makes Claude a genuine ideas partner instead of a generator of three safe suggestions.

Name the type, then pick the shape.
Analysis: material plus questions.
Research: a scoped, cited question.
Drafting: a full brief plus iteration.
Brainstorming: many ideas first, then a shortlist.

The exam guide names these four task types. The tested skill is diagnostic: read the workplace situation, name the type, and brief in the shape of that type. Wrong answers mix up the task types: they apply the briefing of one task type to another task type. Examples are a tightly constrained brainstorm, a one-line research topic, an analysis with no material attached and a draft with no audience. The last example is the recurring wrong answer on drafting. Choosing which product feature or model to use belongs to Domain 3. This objective covers the briefing that follows.
Watch for briefings that suit the wrong task type

Most questions hide the error in a plausible plan that applies the right briefing to the wrong task type. Check each part of a multi-task option separately. One mismatch, such as constraints at the first step of a brainstorm, where you want many ideas, makes the whole option wrong.
The wide-then-narrow sequence of brainstorming is standard facilitation practice, applied to Claude. It is not a rule from a product manual.

[Exam Trap] Asking for an analysis without naming the questions it must answer
Material with no questions attached produces a description of the data, not an analysis. The professional brief supplies the material, the questions, and the decision the findings will inform, and asks for findings, evidence and caveats.
[Exam Trap] Opening a brainstorm with tight constraints and a fixed number of acceptable directions
Constraints applied at the divergence step remove the variety the exercise exists to produce. Criteria belong in the convergence step, where they shortlist a wide field rather than strangling it before it exists.
[Exam Trap] Briefing research as a topic rather than a scoped question

An unscoped topic returns an unfocused report. A research question states the scope, the angle and what the findings must inform, which tells the searching what to investigate and gives the citations claims to support.

A university department administrator has four tasks this week: work out why tutorial attendance dropped this term; learn how three other universities run applicant open days; write the new-term welcome letter to students; and generate ideas for increasing open-day attendance. She intends to use Claude on all four. Which working plan matches strategy to task?
Option ARun every task through Research, since cited sources raise the quality of any output and one consistent method is easier to manage across a busy week
Option BUse Claude for the letter and the ideas only, handling the attendance analysis and the open-day research personally, since those two tasks call for real judgement

Option CAsk Claude why attendance drops at universities generally, answer the open-day comparison from one quick web search, send a one-line request for the welcome letter, and specify exactly three safe, sensible ideas at the start
Option DAttach the attendance data and name the questions for the analysis, give Research a scoped open-day question, brief the letter fully with last year’s letter as the example, and ask for many ideas before shortlisting
[Check Answer]

Reviewing an output means checking what Claude wrote before anyone relies on it. A review asks two questions. Accuracy asks whether the specifics are right: numbers, names, dates, titles, quoted figures, and references to documents or rules. Completeness asks whether anything is missing. A review checks both against the source. The source is the material that Claude used to build the output.
This lesson uses one made-up example throughout: a bakery. Its owner attaches a flour supplier's new contract and asks Claude for a summary. Her business partner will use the summary to decide whether to sign. The summary reads well, but it could contain a wrong price per sack or omit a clause.

Treat every Claude output as a good first draft that can contain errors stated with confidence. The Help Center says why: Claude "can occasionally produce responses that are incorrect or misleading", and users "should not rely on Claude as a singular source of truth". Fluency and confidence are properties of the writing, not evidence about the facts. Claude writes fluently whether it is right or wrong, so an output that reads beautifully has passed no check. The bakery summary would read just as well with a wrong price.

Ownership decides who does the checking. The professional who sends Claude's work owns it. That professional is accountable for it to their team, their members or their funder. Review is the step that changes a draft into work that you can accept responsibility for. Review is not an optional extra for cautious people.

Check the specifics first, in order of consequence. Start with the details that would be most costly or embarrassing if they were wrong. These are usually the figure that a decision depends on, the name at the top of the letter, and the date of the deadline. A draft with twenty accurate sentences and one wrong subtotal is a wrong draft if the meeting decides on that subtotal. At the bakery, the price per sack comes first, because the partner decides on it.

Completeness is harder to check, because the evidence is absent rather than wrong. A fluent summary can omit a section, a theme or a caveat, and nothing in the prose shows the gap. So check the output against the source itself, never against your memory of the source. Follow the source's own structure: its sections, funds, themes or line items. Confirm that each element is either in the output or excluded on purpose. If you read the output alone and accept it, you send it with the gaps still in it. The bakery owner ticks each clause in the contract against the summary.
Check accuracy first every time. A wrong specific is the most likely failure, and it is the quickest to catch. Check completeness second, because that check needs the source open anyway.

When Claude builds an output from attached material, the first check is the attachment. The attachment is already in the conversation, and it takes minutes to compare the two. Anthropic's prompting guidance gives the same advice for long documents: ask Claude to quote the relevant parts of the source before it does the task. In the chat, ask Claude where in the attachment each figure or claim came from. Then spot-check the claims that matter against those locations. An output whose claims trace to the source is checkable in minutes. Do not assume that an output is correct when you cannot trace its claims. The bakery owner asks where the price came from, then reads that clause.

Asking Claude whether it is sure is not a check. The same model that made an error will repeat it with the same confidence, because no new information enters the check. A real check compares the output with its source.

This domain has a larger share of the exam than any other domain, and every objective in it depends on the reviewer's stance. The certification's central claim is that its holder can be trusted with what Claude produces. The holder earns that trust at the review stage, not at the prompting stage. When the stance is right, the other skills in the domain follow from it: spotting failure types, validating claims, knowing when to escalate. The exam treats self-reported confidence as a wrong answer, never as a check.
The register exemplar

The guide's Domain 2 sample question tests this objective. Claude summarises a regulation and cites a specific subsection. The right answer is to verify that citation against the official text before the compliance team sees it. The named wrong answers are trusting Claude's expressed confidence and rewording the summary to sound more formal. Diligence matters more than confidence, and polish is never a substitute for correctness.

[Exam Trap] Sending the output because it reads well or because Claude expressed high confidence
Fluency and confidence are properties of the writing, not evidence about the facts, so neither has checked anything. Compare the output against the source material before anyone relies on it.
[Exam Trap] Asking Claude to confirm its own work and treating a confident yes as review
No new information enters the check: the same model that made an error will repeat it with the same confidence. Compare the output with its source, or ask Claude where in the source each claim came from and spot-check those locations.
[Exam Trap] Verifying one named figure when part of the source may have been dropped

Accuracy checking alone misses the second review question. When the source had more in it than the output shows, review each part of the source's own structure for completeness, not just the details that you noticed.

A scout group treasurer has Claude draft the annual financial summary for the AGM from the group's accounts spreadsheet. The draft reads perfectly, but she must be sure it is right and leaves nothing out, without simply trusting what Claude says. What should the treasurer do before circulating it?
Option ARework the summary into more formal accounting language so that it passes close examination by members at the meeting
Option BCirculate it as it stands: the figures look plausible, the formatting is professional, and the AGM pack deadline is close
Option CAsk Claude whether it is confident the summary is accurate and complete, then circulate the document once Claude says it is

Option DCheck each stated figure against the spreadsheet, then review the list of funds the accounts track to confirm every fund appears in the summary
[Check Answer]

Objective 2.1 gave you the reviewer's stance. This objective names the three failure types a review looks for. A hallucination is content that sounds convincing but is not grounded in fact. An inconsistency is an output that disagrees with itself. Bias is skewed framing, assumptions or language. Each has recognisable signs, and each needs a different response.
This lesson uses one made-up example throughout: a garden centre. Its manager gives Claude three jobs in one week. She wants the steps for the stock report in the till system, a spring sales summary with a table, and appraisal notes for seasonal staff. Each job can fail in one of the three ways.

The Help Center says Claude "can occasionally produce responses that are incorrect or misleading". It "can display quotes that may look authoritative or sound convincing, but are not grounded in fact". That last phrase is the working definition. A hallucination is not vague or hesitant. It appears as an exact-looking figure, a named source or a numbered list of steps. An invented detail has the same confidence as a real one, so specificity is not evidence. For any detail, ask "where would this have come from?" Asking "does this sound right?" tests only the confidence.

Claude can also hallucinate its own capabilities. A separate Help Center article warns that Claude may falsely claim to have sent an email, produced an external document or supplied a working link. Claude has no access to email or file transfer unless they have been explicitly integrated. A claim that Claude has done something outside the conversation is a claim to check. It is not a confirmation that the delivery happened. If Claude says it has emailed the stock figures to the supplier, the manager checks with the supplier.

Hallucination risk depends on grounding: how much material Claude has to work from. The risk is highest where Claude has least to work from:
your organisation's private, internal systems and documents Claude was never given
very recent events that happened after its training data was collected
precise figures that were not in the source material

The highest-risk type of output is a set of confident numbered instructions for an internal tool whose documentation Claude has never seen. These instructions are fluent and specific, but nothing supports them. The stock-report steps are this type of output. Claude names menus in a till system that it was never shown, and some of those menus may not exist. The less grounding Claude could possibly have, the less its specificity means.

h: Inconsistency: The Output Disagrees With Itself
t: You need no external source to detect an inconsistency. One common form is a number in the prose that contradicts the table. Another is a recommendation that contradicts the findings. A third is two sections that give different dates for one event. An internal contradiction is a warning about the reliability of the whole output. It is not a single typo to fix. The process that produced one visible failure was just as able to produce invisible ones. So re-verify the whole output against its source, rather than fixing the one mismatch you noticed and sending the rest. If the spring sales prose and table give different compost figures, the manager checks the whole summary against the till data.

h: Bias: The Pattern, Not the Sentence
t: Bias has the most serious consequences in outputs about people: recruitment material, appraisals, customer descriptions, and anything that ranks or characterises groups. Anthropic's Usage Policy treats employment, housing, finance and healthcare decisions about individuals as high-risk uses. This shows how much is at risk. The skew is in the pattern, so compare the descriptions with each other rather than read sentence by sentence. Suppose the appraisals describe older staff by reliability and younger staff by innovation. No single sentence is objectionable, but the output still is. Look for coded language (words that suggest a group without naming it) and unstated assumptions about age, gender, background or ability. Then apply the read-aloud test: would the framing be acceptable if someone read it aloud to the group that it describes?

The exam tests whether you can distinguish the three failure types and respond to each correctly, because the correct responses differ. For inconsistency, the tested point is the response: re-verify the whole output. Wrong options match a failure type with an incorrect response. They fix one contradiction, delete one biased word, or ask Claude to confirm its own invented steps.
Match the response to the failure type

Verify a hallucination against an authoritative source. When you find an inconsistency, re-verify the whole output. Rework bias as a pattern across the document. Asking "is this right?" on its own is not a check. Anthropic documents two checks. The first is a re-run that you compare against the first output. The second is a follow-up that asks Claude to verify its previous statements and flag what does not fit together. Each check gives you a list of items to check against the source. For the stock-report steps, that source is the till system's documentation.

[Exam Trap] Trusting confident, step-by-step instructions for a private internal system
Claude has no access to an organisation's internal software unless material about it was provided in the conversation, so specific detail with no source behind it is the highest-risk type of hallucination. Treat the steps as unverified and check the system's own documentation.
[Exam Trap] Believing Claude's claim to have sent an email or produced an external file
Claude can hallucinate its capabilities and has no access to tools that are not integrated, so a completion claim is a claim like any other. Verify that the action actually happened rather than treating the statement as confirmation.

[Exam Trap] Fixing the one contradiction you spotted and sending the rest
An internal inconsistency is evidence the output's process failed somewhere, so the whole output needs re-verification against its source. Fixing the one visible contradiction keeps a document that has already shown you it cannot be trusted line by line.
[Exam Trap] Treating bias as one bad word to delete
Bias is in the pattern across descriptions: who gets caveats, whose achievements get qualifiers, which groups are framed in different terms. Deleting a single biased phrase leaves the skew intact, so rework the pattern, not the word.

A skin clinic's practice manager asks Claude how to produce the monthly patient-recall report in the clinic's management software. Claude has had no access to this software or to anything written about it, yet it replies with confident, numbered steps naming specific menus and buttons. She still wants to use Claude for other work that involves this software. What should the manager do with these steps?
Option AFollow the steps as written: detail down to the level of named menus and buttons suggests Claude has reliable knowledge of this software
Option BStop using Claude for anything connected to the clinic’s software, since it has just shown that it will invent plausible instructions rather than admit that it does not know the answer

Option CAsk Claude to double-check each of its steps against the clinic’s software and confirm they are all correct before trying them, so that nothing invented is missed
Option DTreat the steps as unverified and check the software supplier’s documentation or the built-in help instead
[Check Answer]

Validation means checking an output's claims against something that can confirm them. This objective gives the review from objective 2.1 its tools. It puts them in order from the cheapest to the most costly. Your own judgement decides how much checking a given output deserves. A primary document is the original record: the official publication, the regulator's text, the funder's published criteria, the organisation's records.
This lesson uses one made-up example throughout: a removals firm. The office has Claude draft a quote letter from the attached survey notes and price list. The letter states a total price and the council's parking rules for the street. Claude also drafts internal newsletter ideas.

You should not treat Claude as a single source of truth, and high-stakes output deserves careful scrutiny. Claude can produce fluent, specific output that looks correct but is badly mistaken. Specificity alone is not evidence of accuracy.

h: Cheapest First: The Source You Gave It
t: When Claude builds an output from attached material, the first check is the attachment. The attachment is already in the conversation. Each figure, section and claim matches the attachment or does not. This check is the habit from objective 2.1, used as a technique, and it costs minutes. The total is checked against the survey notes and price list. Use a check that takes more effort only when the given source cannot settle the question.

External claims need external checking. The attachments cannot confirm the parking rules, which did not come from them. Web search responses include citations "so you can easily verify sources yourself". Users are advised to cross-reference cited sources and use authoritative ones for critical decisions. The Help Center's hallucination article says to review Claude's cited sources, because checking the original catches misinterpretation. Citations exist to be checked.

The standard is the primary document. A second AI summary, a forum post, or Claude's own earlier output is not independent validation. A check that shares the errors of the thing that it checks proves nothing. For the parking rules, the primary document is the council's published page. Web search from within claude.ai is a legitimate way to find that page. The source validates the claim, never the search.

A traceable output shows where each claim came from, so it is checkable. Do not assume that an output is correct when you cannot trace its claims. For long documents, Anthropic's prompting guidance says to ask Claude to quote the relevant parts of the source before it does its task. For research work, the guidance says to ask Claude to verify information across multiple sources. On the quote letter, ask Claude to show each claim's source and how it reached each conclusion. Then spot-check the important claims. When a decision depends on a single figure, triangulate it: confirm the figure in two independent places before anyone sends it.

The amount of checking depends on what an error would cost. The customer decides on the total, so the total gets two independent confirmations. The newsletter ideas get a read-through. Too little checking of the consequential claim is the obvious failure. Heavy checking on low-stakes work is also wrong, not safe. Time spent on triple checks of newsletter wording that nobody acts on is time not spent on checking the total.

A request that Claude re-check its own output has a limited place. Anthropic's prompting guidance says a self-check catches errors, especially in coding and maths. That guidance names one exception: Claude Opus 5 verifies its own work well without an instruction to do so. A self-check instruction written for earlier models can make Claude Opus 5 verify too much. A self-check is a cheap first check for arithmetic slips and contradictions. It is not independent validation, because the same model misses the same things.

Questions test the techniques. They also test when each technique is proportionate, in both directions. The most common trap is a self-check that looks like verification. An option has the user ask Claude to confirm, re-check or rate its own work, and calls the confident answer validation. The guide's sample rationale says why it fails: self-reported confidence is not a reliable accuracy signal.

[Key Concept] When a validation question offers several checking plans, test each plan against two questions. Does independent information enter the check? Does the depth of checking match what depends on each claim? The right answer passes both. The wrong options usually fail one. Self-check and circular sources (sources that share the errors of what they check) fail independence. Checking every claim to the same maximum depth fails proportionality.

[Exam Trap] Asking Claude to confirm or re-check its claims and calling that verification
No independent information enters the check, and the same errors stay unnoticed. Self-check is a legitimate first check for slips and contradictions, but claims that matter go to an independent source.
[Exam Trap] Checking a claim against another AI summary or Claude's own earlier output
A check against a source made from the thing being checked shares its errors. Check against the primary document instead: the official publication, the published criteria, the organisation's records.
[Exam Trap] Verifying every sentence to the same maximal depth regardless of stakes

The amount of checking depends on what an error would cost. Checking everything to the same full depth spends limited time on prose nothing depends on, which is not the safe choice. Concentrate the checking on the claims a decision rests on.

A heritage railway volunteer coordinator has Claude draft a grant application. The draft states annual visitor numbers, a percentage increase in school visits, and that the railway meets the funder's published eligibility criteria. She has one evening, too little to verify every line in depth, and nothing may depend on Claude's statements alone. What is the right validation plan before submission?
Option AAsk Claude to re-check the whole draft carefully and confirm each claim, then submit once it confirms its figures
Option BCheck the visitor numbers against the railway’s own records, recalculate the percentage from those records, and check the eligibility claims against the funder’s published criteria document

Option CIndependently verify every sentence in the application to the same depth, including the descriptive history section, before anyone sees it
Option DCheck the eligibility claims against the summary of the criteria that Claude produced earlier in the conversation, and confirm the visitor figures are consistent everywhere they appear across the whole draft
[Check Answer]

Escalation passes a Claude output to a qualified person to review before anyone uses it. Triage is the decision about who reviews each output. Triggers are properties of the situation that raise the cost of an error. This objective covers when your own review is not enough. It also covers whose review is enough in that case.
This lesson uses one made-up example throughout: a driving school. Its owner has four Claude drafts: a website advert, a refund reply under the booking terms, appraisal notes on an instructor, and a car-cleaning reminder. All four read well.

Each trigger below needs qualified human review.
an external audience: customers, the public, press, funders
legal, financial or contractual consequence
decisions about people: hiring, appraisal, allocation
safety or health implications
output that is irreversible once sent
One trigger is enough reason for a review by a second, qualified person. When several triggers apply together, escalation is mandatory. Confidence and polish are not on the list, because every Claude draft already has them. Claude is not a single source of truth, and high-stakes output deserves careful scrutiny.

At the driving school, the advert has an external audience. The refund reply has a contractual consequence. The appraisal notes inform a decision about a person. The cleaning reminder has none of these triggers, so the owner reviews it herself.
You review outputs with no trigger yourself, carefully, using the habits from objectives 2.1 to 2.3. These outputs are internal working material, first drafts that will change in later versions, and routine low-consequence messages. That review is real. It is not a way to skip review. Triage decides who reviews, never whether anyone reviews.

Anthropic's Usage Policy sets the standard. It names High-risk Areas, such as legal, medical, financial and employment matters. In these areas, Claude's output can become advice to a person or a decision about them. The policy calls that output a High-risk AI Recommendation. It requires two things for it. The person must be told that AI was used, and a qualified person must review it. The review rule reads: "A qualified person must meaningfully review a High-risk AI Recommendation, with the authority to change or modify it, before it is delivered as advice". The same rule applies before the recommendation is used to make a decision. Advising someone on their legal rights, or on what to do in a specific legal matter, is one of these areas.

A qualified person is "someone with the training or experience to evaluate the output in that field". The words that pick the reviewer are "in that field". Contract language goes to someone with legal competence. Tax figures go to the accountant. Clinical claims go to the clinician. Hiring criteria go to HR judgement. Outside the High-risk Areas, the policy sets no review rule, but competence is still the test that picks the reviewer.
Seniority and availability are neither necessary nor sufficient. An unqualified reader, however senior, cannot catch the errors that make the content dangerous. A busy director who skim-reads a lease clause gives reassurance, not review. The refund reply goes to a solicitor, not to the owner.

Under-escalation, too little escalation, is the intuitive failure. It sends content to an external audience when that content makes claims with professional consequences, because the draft reads authoritatively. Or it accepts an output as "only internal" when that output informs an external or consequential decision. Claude's output reads authoritatively by default. But the triggers belong to the situation, and the polish does not remove them. The next destination of the output decides more than the place where Claude drafted it. The appraisal notes stay in the office but inform a decision about an instructor.

Over-escalation feels safe because caution feels safe. It is not safe. One example is a committee for a rota note. Another is a professional reviewer for every routine draft. Each adds more process than the work needs. Over-escalation overloads reviewers, delays routine work and teaches the organisation to ignore the escalation channel that high-stakes outputs need. A solicitor who reads the cleaning reminder reaches the refund reply later. The skill is triage, not maximal caution.

In this objective, the reasons to escalate are quality and stakes. These are what happens if the output is wrong, and who is competent to catch the errors. Domain 6 covers other reasons to stop: the data is personal or regulated, or the use is outside organisational AI policy. Both kinds of reason can arise in one situation, such as a refund reply that quotes a pupil's personal data, but the trigger differs. The programme's technical escalation is a third kind. It hands a task to a Claude Developer or Architect because the task needs automation or integration. In that case, the task needs more than the chat can give. It is not a case of an output that needs a qualified reviewer.

The exam tests this objective as triage: a decision based on the triggers that the output has, not on how polished it looks. It penalises a wrong decision in either direction. In the questions, look for the destination and for what qualifies a named reviewer. Candidates rarely expect the exam to test over-escalation, and "escalate everything" is a real wrong answer. The exam keeps Domain 6 triggers distinct.
[Key Concept] Triage asks two questions in order. Which triggers does this output have? If it has any, who is qualified in that subject to catch the errors that matter? The wrong options answer with rank, availability or a process that applies to every output.

[Exam Trap] Choosing the reviewer by seniority or availability
Where the Usage Policy requires review, a qualified person must do it: someone with the training or experience to evaluate the output in that field. A senior manager's sign-off on legal wording is reassurance, not review. Choose whoever can catch the dangerous error.
[Exam Trap] Letting output pass unchecked because it is only internal
The trigger is what the output carries, not where it first goes. An internal analysis that feeds an external bid or a decision about people carries the consequence with it, so escalate on the destination and the stakes, not the label.
[Exam Trap] Escalating everything to be safe

Over-escalation is a tested wrong answer, not a cautious right one. Routing routine internal drafts through committees or professionals overloads reviewers and weakens the escalation channel that high-stakes outputs need; careful self-review suffices for genuinely low-stakes material.

An opticians' practice manager has three Claude drafts: advertising copy for a new lens range claiming specific visual outcomes, a reworded internal rota-swap policy, and a reply to a patient complaint that touches on what may have gone wrong clinically. The manager has no clinical training and does not know what eye-care advertising may legally promise. Each draft must be checked by someone who knows its subject, with no needless delay. What is the right triage?
Option APublish the advertising copy, since it reads professionally and was drafted from the product literature, and ask the optometrist to look over the rota policy and complaint reply

Option BPut all three drafts to the practice’s weekly management meeting for collective sign-off before any of them is used, so that responsibility for every document is shared by the whole team
Option CQualified review before either goes out (a health-claims expert for the advertising claims, the optometrist for the complaint reply), and the manager’s own careful read for the rota policy
Option DReview all three personally and carefully as the accountable manager, then send them, keeping turnaround fast and responsibility in one place
[Check Answer]

Editing an output means deciding what reaches the reader, and in what form. Adapting means changing the delivery for one reader while keeping the substance. Earlier objectives in this domain asked whether an output is right. This objective asks whether it is right for its reader. That judgement is editorial, and it is yours. Claude drafts, and you edit.
This lesson uses one made-up example throughout: a veterinary practice that asks Claude for a discharge note to a dog's owner after surgery. The draft is accurate but clinical, and the warning signs are halfway down page two.

Claude's draft is unfinished material. Official documentation describes Claude as a partner for drafting and rewriting. Claude can produce anything from an email to a screenplay, and it can rework its answers on request. Claude does not make the final decision. That decision covers what stays, what goes, whether the emphasis is right, and whether this audience will understand and act on the result.

You have two remedies. You can edit the output yourself, or you can direct a revision that names what must change. A directed revision gives Claude follow-up instructions, not a bare request to try again. Knowing which remedy fits is part of the skill. At the practice, moving the warning signs higher is a quick edit. A plain-language rewrite is a revision that you direct.

The exam tests whether you recognise that a technically correct output is wrong for its reader. Typical cases are jargon for a non-specialist audience, detail-heavy analysis for an executive with little time, and an internal register (the style of language used inside the organisation) in a customer-facing note. A reader who cannot understand a document cannot act on it. Adapting changes three things. The vocabulary becomes simpler, to match the reader's level. Each sentence holds less information. The order changes so that the urgent item comes first, not in the middle of the document.

Adaptation fails in two directions, both tested. Leaving output that is hard for the reader untouched because it is correct fails the reader. Removing the substance while simplifying fails them too: to make the text easier to read, a serious point is softened until the reader cannot see it. The findings, the recommendations and the costs must stay in the text after any adaptation. A friendly note that drops the warning signs has failed the owner. After adapting, check the new version against the original for anything lost or softened.

When choosing between versions, set the criteria before reading: accuracy preserved, audience fit, tone, completeness, length. Read each version against the list. Defend your choice with the criteria, not with the style. A comparison without criteria chooses the prettiest prose by default. Style is the only comparison that fluent output always wins. So in a comparison without criteria, a fluent version with less content beats a correct one.
Three criteria are usually enough. For the practice, the criteria are: nothing factual lost, the right register for the owner, and warning signs first. The criteria must exist before you read either version, because criteria set afterwards tend to justify the version you already liked.

Claude produces versions in different registers, lengths and structures, and says how they differ. You apply the criteria and choose a version. The practice does this when it chooses between a short note and a long one. Asking Claude which of its versions is better gives Claude the judgement that this objective certifies. Claude's assessment of its own work is not a reliable signal either. Objective 2.3 covers this limitation. In Artifacts, document versions appear side by side, and earlier versions remain retrievable. So Artifacts suit this pattern.

The guide describes Associate-level professionals as distinguished by their ability to critically evaluate AI-generated content and adapt outputs for different audiences.
Giving Claude clearer feedback so that the next draft improves is objective 1.3, prompt refinement. Assessing, adapting and finishing the output that you already have is this objective. Improving the practice's prompt for future notes is 1.3. Fixing this note is 2.5. To distinguish the two objectives, read the action that the question tests.
The clue in comparison questions

When a question offers two versions and asks which to send, look at the basis that each option uses for the comparison. Options that choose by flow, tone or general appeal are wrong. The right answer sets criteria first, checks both versions against them, and then chooses on that basis. Fluency is never one of the criteria, because both versions already have it.

[Exam Trap] Sending an accurate but hard-to-read output because the content is correct
A reader who cannot understand the document cannot act on it, and the urgent point stays hard to find. Adapt the delivery for the named reader while keeping the substance.
[Exam Trap] Adapting for a lay audience by cutting the difficult content
The findings, recommendations and costs are what the reader needs to act on. Softening a serious point until the reader cannot see it fails the reader. Put the substance into plain words rather than deleting it, then check the result against the original.
[Exam Trap] Asking Claude to pick its own best version and sending its choice

Claude generates the versions and explains how they differ, but the choice of what goes out belongs to the person sending it. Its self-reported confidence is not a reliable accuracy signal. Apply your criteria and choose.
[Exam Trap] Choosing between two versions by which reads better, with no criteria fixed beforehand
Style is the only comparison that fluent output always wins, so a fluent version with less content beats a correct one. Fix the criteria before reading, then judge each version against them.

A building surveyor's assistant has a survey summary that is accurate but dense with structural terminology, and the urgent roof defect sits mid-document. It must go to the buyers: first-time buyers with no construction background. The surveyor insists that the buyers can follow every finding and that the assistant, rather than Claude, settles the final wording. What is the right way to prepare it?
Option AHave Claude produce two adapted versions, ask it which one works better for first-time buyers, and send the version that it recommends
Option BCut the technical sections down to a short, reassuring overview so the buyers get an easy read without the intimidating detail

Option CSend it to the buyers unchanged: the findings are accurate as they stand, and simplifying technical content for lay readers risks misstating the surveyor’s professional conclusions in a document they may rely on
Option DDirect a plain-language revision that keeps every defect, recommendation and cost, moves the roof issue to the top, then check the adapted version against the original for anything softened or lost
[Check Answer]

A long, productive conversation is not a deliverable. Its findings, decisions and usable text are mixed with failed approaches and replaced drafts. Two deliberate acts turn the conversation into a deliverable, and neither act happens automatically. Curation extracts what the deliverable needs. Format selection gives the deliverable the container that its reader will use: an inline chat response, a structured table or an artifact. An artifact is substantial, standalone content that Claude puts in a dedicated window, separate from the conversation.

This lesson uses one made-up example throughout: a plumbing firm. Its office manager has spent weeks planning winter work with Claude. Three outputs are due. A customer wants to know today whether the boiler service includes a flue check. The owner must choose between three boiler suppliers on price, warranty and delivery time. The plumbers need the winter call-out procedure, which the firm revises every autumn.

h: From Working Material to Work Product
t:
Curation starts from the deliverable, not the conversation. Ask who reads it, what they do with it, and whether it will be reused or revised. Then extract exactly what that reader needs, and shape it into its final container. Forwarding the whole conversation, or leaving the deliverable scattered across it, delegates the curation to the reader. The reader will not do the curation. So next month's colleague scrolls thirty screenfuls and searches for the decisions.
Most of a working conversation is scaffolding: material that helped you reach the decisions. So curation is selective on purpose. The deliverable gives its reader the decisions alone. The plumbers get the final call-out steps, not the drafts.

The Help Center's definition of artifacts is also the selection rule. Artifacts suit significant, self-contained content you are likely to edit, iterate on or reuse outside the conversation. The opposite of this rule defines the other two containers.
An inline chat response fits quick, one-off answers that the reader uses at once: a fact, a short explanation, text to paste and send immediately. A structured table fits anything the reader compares or scans: options against criteria, items with consistent attributes, schedules. If the reader needs rows and columns, prose is the wrong container. An artifact fits a standalone document, plan or reference page that stays in use: it is revised, reused or shared as a thing in itself.

The choice follows the reader's use: inline for content the reader uses once, a table for content the reader compares and scans, and an artifact for content the reader reuses and revises. So the flue-check answer goes inline, the supplier choice becomes a table with the criteria as columns, and the call-out procedure becomes an artifact.

An artifact is useful because of what happens after the first draft. You can ask Claude to change it, or you can edit a document, deck or design directly. The deliverable then changes as one thing, not as fragments that you paste again into the chat. To try a different direction without losing what you have, edit an earlier message. Editing an earlier message creates a different version of the chat with its own artifacts. The original version stays where it was. When you share the artifact, it gets a link that other people can open.

For shared work, a colleague who receives a runbook next year opens the current document. Next autumn, the plumbing firm's manager opens one revised call-out procedure. The format choice is also reversible, and it is always your decision. If useful content arrived inline, one message that asks Claude to convert it into an artifact is enough.

Each wrong format has a predictable cost. A reusable runbook that stays as plain text in the chat is lost and then created again. A comparison delivered as paragraphs makes every reader rebuild the table in their head, and some rebuild it wrongly. Putting everything in a table puts judgements that need full sentences into cells that are too small for them. Putting everything in an artifact adds needless formality to one-off answers, such as the flue-check reply. Choose the format by the reader's use, never by habit.

The exam tests format selection through these failure modes. This objective is about choosing the shape of the output. Choosing the product feature or model for the task is Domain 3. That domain covers a Project for recurring context, Research for a cited report, and which model to use. A format question may mention those features in its scenario. The right answer is always about the container the reader receives.

[Key Concept] For every output, ask one question: what does the reader do with this? Read it once, compare across it, or return to it? The answer decides the format, and it overrides every default. Exam questions reward matching each output to its use. They penalise both prose chosen without thought and structure added automatically.
Current state: artifacts changed in September 2026

Anthropic reworked artifacts on 16 September 2026. They are now designs, decks, documents, dashboards and small tools made in any conversation. Artifacts made in a chat before that date are "legacy": they can still be opened and shared, but no more can be made. The earlier Help Center article described a version selector for switching versions. The current article, checked 28 September 2026, no longer documents one. The exam guide names artifacts only as an output format, so no right answer depends on that control. Where these lessons talk about comparing versions, they mean the branching described above.

[Exam Trap] Answering a format question with Projects, Research mode or a model choice
Choosing the product feature or model for the task is Domain 3. When a question asks how information should be organised or delivered, the answer is about the output's container: inline, table or artifact, matched to the reader's use.
[Exam Trap] Defaulting every output to the same container
Artifacts for everything add needless formality to one-off answers, and tables for everything force narrative judgement into cells. Options that use one format for everything sound systematic and safe, which makes them tempting. Vary the format with the use.
[Exam Trap] Sharing the whole conversation instead of curating the deliverable

Forwarding weeks of working material delegates the curation to readers who will not do it: the decisions stay hidden among failed approaches and superseded drafts. Extract what each reader needs into the container that fits their use.

A swimming club's gala organiser has weeks of Claude conversations about the annual gala. Three outputs are now needed: the agreed start time for tonight's committee question, a comparison of three candidate dates against pool availability, volunteer numbers and fixture clashes, and the gala-day runbook that will be revised and reused every year. She wants each in the simplest form its use allows, and her successor must be able to receive the runbook and edit it. Which formats fit?
Option ACreate artifacts for all three outputs so that nothing is lost and every answer stays permanently available in one dedicated place the whole committee can open

Option BReply to all three needs in chat prose and share the conversation with the committee, so that members can read the full context and history behind each answer for themselves
Option CAnswer the start time inline, put the three dates in a table with the criteria as columns, and build the runbook as an artifact revised in place each year
Option DPut all three outputs into tables, since structured formats are easier to scan than prose, and a committee that is short of time can find each answer very quickly
[Check Answer]

Claude offers four ways to handle work. Ordinary chat is a single conversation. The Help Center describes Projects as self-contained workspaces with their own chat histories and knowledge bases. Research is for questions whose answer must be assembled from several outside sources, and it returns a cited report. An artifact is standalone content displayed in its own window, beside the conversation. Most people pick a feature by habit. Identify the kind of task instead, before writing any prompt.

This lesson uses one made-up example throughout: a hair salon. Its owner has four jobs. She needs one reply to a client's complaint. Each week she writes booking reminders from the same price list and house style. She wants to know how other salons handle no-show deposits, with sources her partner can check. She revises an aftercare sheet for her stylists every quarter. Four questions sort the jobs. Is the work one-off or recurring? Does it stand alone, or does it need the same standing context (background information that stays the same) again and again? Is it consumed once, or revised and reused? Can Claude answer from what you supply, or must the answer be gathered from outside sources? Each feature exists for one kind of task.

A single question, a single draft or an analysis of a document attached during the chat needs no workspace, agentic search (Research, which builds a cited answer from several sources) or separate artifact window. Ordinary chat handles such a task immediately. Ordinary chat is the right choice more often than enthusiasts admit. The complaint reply is this kind of task.

A Project has two assets that persist across chats. Its instructions shape Claude's responses in every chat inside the workspace. Its knowledge base holds uploaded material Claude uses as background for those chats. You configure both assets once, and then both apply to every chat in the Project. The signal is a need for the same background documents, standing preferences and working material across many conversations. Re-pasting the same context into chat after chat is a Project's work done by hand. Projects exist to end that workaround. A Project would hold the price list and house style the salon owner re-pastes each week.

In Research, Claude works agentically. It runs multiple searches, and later searches use what earlier searches found. Its synthesised report includes citations so that the findings can be checked. The signals are a survey of a whole field, a brief on how others do something, and an overview of the current state. Another signal is an audience who will want to see where the findings came from. The deposit question fits Research. Research is not a quality upgrade for ordinary questions. A task answerable from material you already hold gains nothing from Research, because nothing needs gathering.

h: Artifacts: Work with Its Own Life
t: Claude creates an artifact when the output is significant, self-contained and likely to be edited, iterated on or reused outside the conversation. That last condition is the dominant signal: the work is used beyond the chat that produced it. Examples are a reference sheet revised every quarter and a plan that will be shared and updated. Each should exist as one evolving version, not as fragments scattered through a conversation history. You iterate an artifact in one of two ways. You ask Claude to change it, or you edit an earlier message. Editing an earlier message creates a branch of the chat with artifacts of its own. You can return to an artifact and share a finished one. The aftercare sheet fits this signal.

Real work mixes the features. A Project can contain chats that produce artifacts. A Research report can be the basis of an artifact document that is revised each quarter. The salon's deposit report might be the basis of a deposit policy artifact.

This objective tests whether you pick a feature by reading the task. The exam does not test the combinations. Each question presents one piece of work with one dominant signal: recurring context, multi-source citation, iterative deliverable or simple one-off. The wrong answers are always real features applied to the wrong kind of task. Do not dismiss ordinary chat, because the exam treats it as a right answer. When a question's dominant signal is a simple one-off, ordinary chat is the professional answer, however capable the other features are. The exam is willing to make the plainest option the right answer.

Writing a Project's instructions and curating its knowledge base belong to Domain 5. In this objective, the exam tests whether you recognise the recurrence. Checking a Research report's citations belongs to Domain 2. Choosing between an inline answer, a table and a document is Domain 2's format question. In this objective, an artifact is the place for iterative, reusable work.
[Key Concept] Find the dominant signal first, and then choose the feature that matches it. Recurring shared context means a Project. A cited multi-source answer means Research. An output that is revised and reused means an artifact. A self-contained one-off means ordinary chat.

[Exam Trap] Treating an artifact as the place to keep standing context for new chats
An artifact is a container for one evolving output; it does not give new conversations standing context. A Project's instructions and knowledge base apply from the start of every chat, so nothing needs pasting in.
[Exam Trap] Running everything through a Project or Research to maximise quality
The most elaborate feature is not the safest choice. A simple one-off gains nothing from a workspace or a multi-source report. Ordinary chat is a legitimate answer in this objective. The dominant signal decides, not the feature's prestige.
[Exam Trap] Treating re-pasting the same context into every chat as diligence

The manual workaround repeats a Project's setup work every single time instead of once. When a scenario describes the same documents and preferences supplied chat after chat, the answer moves that work into a Project.

A parish council clerk has four pieces of work: the monthly agenda-and-minutes cycle that always needs the council's standing orders, member list and format conventions; a one-off briefing on how five nearby councils run allotment waiting lists, with sources the councillors can check; a single resident's question about a grant deadline; and an emergency-contacts sheet that is revised every quarter and shared with all members. She wants nothing more elaborate than each piece needs, no Project for work that never recurs, and nothing re-supplied by hand. Which plan matches feature to work?

Option ARun everything in ordinary chat, pasting the standing orders and member list in each month and rebuilding the contacts sheet from the old conversation each quarter
Option BA Project for the monthly agenda-and-minutes cycle, Research for the five-councils briefing, ordinary chat for the grant deadline question, and the contacts sheet built and revised as an artifact
Option CCreate one Project holding all four pieces of work, since keeping every council task inside a single workspace is simpler than making a separate feature decision for each individual piece as it comes up

Option DUse Research for both the allotments briefing and the grant deadline question, and publish every output as a shareable artifact so that all four pieces of council work carry the same maximum level of rigour
[Check Answer]

This objective names three model families: Haiku, Sonnet and Opus. Each family is a tier. The tiers make a real trade-off of speed and cost against depth of reasoning. The Haiku family is the lowest-cost tier. Anthropic lists it as the fastest and describes it as built for high-volume, latency-sensitive tasks. The Opus family is the most capable reasoning tier, for complex, high-stakes work. The Sonnet family offers the best combination of speed and intelligence: the balanced middle and the sensible everyday default. No tier is "the good one". Each tier is the right choice for work that matches its strengths.
