This lesson uses one made-up example throughout: a florist that has two jobs for Claude. One is standardising three hundred product listings into one website template. The other is reconciling two wholesalers' reports that partly disagree into one ordering recommendation.

The most capable tier takes longer for each response. Your choice of model is one of the factors that determine how quickly a usage allowance is consumed. The fastest tier is fast because it is not built for the most demanding work. On Opus, every florist listing would take longer for no gain.

Capability means depth on demanding work. That depth covers resolving ambiguity and contradiction, multi-step reasoning, synthesis across sources that partly disagree, and drafting where a subtle error has real consequences. Capability does not mean better at everything, so the top tier is not the universal choice. For routine, well-specified work, the lighter tiers (the faster, lower-cost ones) produce what the task needs, faster. The florist's listings are routine. The wholesaler recommendation is not routine.
Never claim a lighter tier matches a heavier tier's quality on demanding work. The documentation does not claim it. Use a lighter tier because it fits the task and its output is reviewed, never because the quality is equal.

h: Reading the Signals in a Task
t: Lighter-tier signals are high volume, a routine and repetitive shape, simple transformation, speed that matters, and outputs that are individually low-stakes. Examples of simple transformation are reformatting, extracting or standardising. Those outputs are still spot-checked, because the review discipline from Domain 2 never stops. Signals for the most capable tier are ambiguity, contradiction to resolve, judgement with consequences and complex synthesis. Another signal is work where a wrong subtle conclusion costs more than the extra time. When neither set dominates, the balanced middle is the everyday answer.

h: Reading the Signals in a Task
t: Size does not decide the tier. The kind of work decides it. Standardising a long list of entries into one template is lighter-tier work however many rows it has. Reconciling two reports that partly disagree into a single recommendation is capable-tier work however short the final page is. The florist's listings go to a lighter tier, and a sample of them is checked. The one-page recommendation goes to Opus.

You choose the model in the chat interface, not in technical configuration. Click the model name and choose another available model. You can change it at any point in a conversation, and the change applies from Claude's next response. The model picker shows the models your account has access to. That list varies by plan and, in workplaces, by what an organisation has enabled.

So the tier decision is not a one-off commitment. Routine preparation can run on a lighter tier, and the hard synthesis can run on the most capable tier, inside one piece of work. The florist can extract each wholesaler's terms on Haiku, then switch to Opus for the recommendation. Never opening the model picker serves the average task. It serves both the routine end and the demanding end badly. A default model is a setting on your account, not a decision about your work.

The guide names the three families. The objective exists because no tier suits every task. It tests whether you read a task's actual demands, not its prestige. That skill remains useful after any change to the set of models. In the guide's own sample question, the right answer for a high volume of short, routine drafts, where speed and cost matter more than deep reasoning, is the faster, lower-cost model. "Always use the top model" is a named wrong answer.
Choosing by a project's importance

"This project is important" does not move a routine task to the top tier. Importance belongs to projects. Demands belong to tasks. The right answer is the tier that matches the current task. A routine reformat inside an important project is still a routine reformat.
Specific model names and the current line-up change over time and belong on the quick reference.

[Exam Trap] Choosing the most capable model for everything because the work is important
Always using the top model wastes the cost and latency budget on work that does not need it. Routine high-volume work does not need depth, and a project's importance does not make every task inside it demanding.
[Exam Trap] Sending work that plainly needs depth to the fastest tier because it is just writing
This saving costs more in the end. Quality demands depend on the cost of being wrong: a short output that carries judgement, contradiction or consequences is exactly where the extra time of the capable tier is worth it, however quick the typing would be.
[Exam Trap] Accepting a claim that the lighter tier gives the same quality on demanding work

No documentation says a lighter tier matches a heavier one on demanding work; fitness for the task plus review justifies it. The exam guide reserves the most capable model for complex reasoning. Current docs (October 2026) advise moving up when top effort settings fall short.

A community energy co-operative employs one administrator, who has two jobs side by side: standardising six hundred member records into one address format, and drafting the co-op response to a complex regulatory consultation where three board members have given partly contradictory advice. She must keep spending on the routine job as low as she can, without risking the quality of the co-op's position. How should she assign models?
Option AUse the most capable model for the member records, since data accuracy matters at that scale, and the fastest model for the consultation response, since a single letter is quick to produce

Option BUse the fastest model for both jobs, since the records are routine and the consultation response is just plain drafting once all three board views are pasted in
Option CUse the most capable model for both jobs, since the reputation of the co-op with all its members depends on this work and the best model maximises quality everywhere
Option DRun the six hundred records on the fastest, lower-cost model and spot-check a sample, and draft the regulatory consultation response on the most capable model
[Check Answer]

Objective 3.2 taught what the tiers are. Every choice between them affects three things, which this lesson calls currencies: cost, speed and quality. Cost is the plan's usage allowance, not a per-use invoice. Speed is the wait for each response. You feel that wait most sharply across many runs. Quality is depth on demanding work, as objective 3.2 defines it: handling ambiguity, reconciling contradiction and making judgements safely. The skill is to name the currency that a task needs, and then to spend only that currency.

This lesson uses one made-up example throughout: a fish and chip shop. Its owner uses Claude for two jobs. One is five hundred review replies that vary only in a name and a dish. The other is one response to the council after a hygiene inspection.

Ask three questions in order. What does being wrong cost here? How many times will this run? Who is waiting for the answer? The answers name the currency. Without the answers, the choice is a feeling rather than a decision with named requirements. For the shop's replies, an error is cheap, the job runs five hundred times and nobody is waiting. For the hygiene response, an error is costly, the job runs once and the council is waiting.

The Help Center lists model choice, effort level, current conversation length and file attachment size among the factors that determine how quickly usage is consumed. The allowance is finite, so every task that you overpay for takes allowance from the tasks that are still to come. Review replies on the heaviest model use allowance that the hygiene response needs.

If a job runs once, the difference between tiers is seconds and a very small part of the allowance. If it runs five hundred times, the same difference decides whether the job finishes today. It also decides whether the allowance lasts the week. High-volume routine work, like the review replies, belongs on the lighter tier.
Volume work on a fast tier gets a sampled spot-check, because Domain 2's duty to verify never stops. The spot-check is sized to the job: the owner reads a sample of the replies. The fast tier plus the spot-check makes the choice professional rather than merely cheap.

Stakes act on a different currency: quality. Some single outputs are inputs to a decision with consequences, and they need depth. Such outputs include a regulatory submission, a legally sensitive letter and a recommendation that a board will act on. The seconds that a lighter tier saves are worth nothing against the cost of a subtly wrong conclusion. "It is only one letter" is true and irrelevant, because one letter with consequences demands more than five hundred letters without consequences. Quality requirements depend on the cost of being wrong, not the prestige of the task. Then a qualified human reviews the high-stakes output, whatever model drafted it. The hygiene response gets the capable tier and a qualified checker.

Real workloads mix shapes. Split them by their demands rather than run everything at one setting. Put the routine bulk on the fast tier with sampled review. Put the difficult core on the capable tier with proper review. The model picker makes the split easy. You can change the model at any point in a conversation, and the change applies from the next response.

Three wrong answers recur. The first is maximum quality everywhere. It spends depth on work that does not need it, and the waste grows with the volume. The second is minimum cost everywhere. It delivers shallow output on the work whose errors are expensive. The third is the escalation loop, which re-runs a disappointing output on heavier and heavier models. The loop treats a vague brief as a model problem, but a vague brief fails at every tier. Fixing the brief belongs to Domain 1, and no tier upgrade replaces that fix. If the hygiene brief never names its reader, every tier fails.

Exam questions ask you to judge what a real task needs in the three currencies. In the guide's sample question, the right answer is a faster, lower-cost model for straightforward, high-volume drafting. The usual trap is a decision about stakes that is argued with reasons about volume.
[Key Concept] Volume multiplies cost and speed. Stakes multiply quality. When a question mixes both kinds of work, the right answer almost always splits the workload. The bulk gets the fast tier plus sampled review. The piece that carries consequences gets the capable tier plus proper review.

[Exam Trap] Justifying the fast tier on a high-stakes output because it is only one letter
Stakes, not volume, set the quality requirement. One output that informs a consequential decision needs more than hundreds of routine ones do, and the seconds saved by the lighter tier are worthless against the cost of a subtly wrong conclusion.
[Exam Trap] Justifying the top tier on routine bulk because the work is important
Importance does not transfer from a project to every task inside it. Routine transformation at volume needs speed and cost kept low, with a sampled check; using the most capable model hundreds of times over gives nothing the task needs.
[Exam Trap] Escalating to a heavier model when the real defect is a vague brief
A vague brief fails at every tier, so each heavier re-run spends usage allowance and waiting time and still misses. Fixing the brief belongs to Domain 1. Check the brief before changing the model.

A regional athletics association is preparing its annual awards night: five hundred personalised invitation letters that vary only in name, club and event, and one difficult letter to a club being suspended for a safeguarding failure, where tone, precision and care about legal risk all matter. Spending on the invitations must stay as low as possible, and nothing that would make the suspension letter safer may be skimped. How should the administrator run the two jobs?
Option ARun the five hundred invitations on the faster, lower-cost model and spot-check a sample, then draft the suspension letter on the most capable model with qualified human review before it is sent

Option BDraft the suspension letter on the faster model to conserve usage, and if the tone misses, re-run the same prompt on the most capable model, repeating until an acceptable version of the letter finally appears
Option CRun both jobs on the most capable model, since the awards night is the most important event of the association and nothing about it should look second-rate
Option DRun both jobs on the faster model, since the invitations are obvious volume work and the suspension letter is only one letter, easily handled by any model
[Check Answer]

A conversation holds a finite working space. Everything said, attached and produced so far is what Claude is working with. Very long conversations approach the platform's length and usage limits, and longer ones consume more of the usage allowance. Separately, claude.ai has memory across chats. Chat search is prompted retrieval, where you ask Claude to find something in past conversations.
This lesson uses one made-up example throughout: a greengrocer who has planned the shop's Christmas veg boxes in one very long chat since August. The chat holds supplier choices, three abandoned box designs, the agreed contents and a much-revised price list.

When a conversation reaches its length limit, the official guidance gives two options. Start a new conversation, or use a Project to work with larger amounts of information. Treat a long conversation like a long meeting. Know that it will end, and decide what must remain after it ends.

Restart when a piece of work is done, when the chat holds abandoned approaches and superseded drafts, or when it nears its limits. A marathon chat is a very long chat. It carries everything that has ever been in it, including the greengrocer's three abandoned designs. A clean start with exactly the right context is better than a marathon chat.
Summarise before you leave the chat: have Claude summarise the decisions made, the current state and what remains. Then verify the summary yourself against the source records. The summary contains every uncorrected error from the chat that it summarises. The greengrocer verifies her summary against supplier emails and invoices. The verified summary becomes the new chat's opening brief.

Persist any specific working output that the next conversation will need. Paste it into the next conversation, re-attach the file, or store it in Project knowledge, where every chat in the Project starts with it. A standing document that keeps being revised and shared has a fourth place: an artifact. In an artifact, you iterate on the document as one evolving version. The greengrocer pastes the agreed contents into the new chat. She makes the staff's weekly price list an artifact, and she stores the supplier list in Project knowledge.

h: What Memory Carries, and What It Does Not
t: Memory is built as a set of individual topics: your role, your projects, your communication preferences, your ongoing work context. It is context about you, not transcripts, drafts or attached documents. Each Project has its own memory. Inside a Project, Claude also uses your memory from chats outside Projects, but never another Project's memory. So memory saves you the work of introducing yourself again. Memory does not reliably carry an approved outline or a data file into the next chat. The greengrocer's new chat may know her shop, but the price list is in the new chat only because she persisted it.

h: What Memory Carries, and What It Does Not
t: Two out-of-date claims are wrong here, in opposite directions. One claim is that Claude cannot remember anything across chats. The other is that you can trust memory to carry a working document. Persisting a specific working output explicitly remains the dependable pattern.

This objective tests planning, not repair of damage, and the exam expects you to be precise about what memory holds. Check the question's time frame. A planning question describes work organised for what comes next. Examples include a long piece of work approaching limits, a project entering its final phase and a handover being planned. The greengrocer's case is a planning case. A chat that already produces poor outputs, where you diagnose the problem after it has happened, belongs to Domain 7. The same marathon chat can appear in both kinds of question. The right answer follows the question that the scenario asks. Here the right answer is the proactive practice. Restart deliberately. Summarise, and verify the summary (Domain 2 does not stop at handover). Persist what the next conversation depends on.

Nothing in the official guidance claims that the product degrades in long chats. No right answer relies on that claim. Rollout dates and plan availability are dated facts, and they are on this domain's quick reference.
The false belief that a new chat loses all context
"A new conversation would lose all our context" is the best argument for the marathon chat, and it is false. A verified summary and persisted documents carry the context that is worth keeping into the new conversation. They do this at a fraction of the length and the usage.

[Exam Trap] Relying on memory or chat search to carry a specific working output into a new chat
Memory holds context about you as individual topics, not transcripts, drafts or attachments, and chat search is prompted retrieval. A working output the next conversation depends on is transferred by explicit persistence: paste it, re-attach it, or store it in Project knowledge.
[Exam Trap] Pasting an unverified summary into the new conversation as the efficient handover
The summary contains every uncorrected error in the chat it summarises. Check it against the source records before the new chat relies on it, and paste agreed wording in word for word.
[Exam Trap] Keeping everything in one enormous chat because a restart would lose the context

This is the habit of keeping one marathon chat, presented as continuity. The chat fills with superseded drafts and abandoned approaches alongside the decisions that matter, approaches length limits, and consumes more usage; summarising and persisting move everything worth keeping into the new chat.

A wedding coordinator has run one enormous conversation across three months of planning: venue decisions, the running order, the readings, corrections to names. The final month starts now, the chat is full of superseded detail, and the platform length limits are close. Some names and dates were corrected more than once, so any summary of the old chat may carry an outdated version. What is the best plan?
Option AStart a fresh conversation and rely on memory and chat search to carry the seating plan and running order across, asking Claude to remember the planning details, including the corrected names and readings, before closing down the old three-month chat

Option BHave Claude summarise decisions and open questions, verify that summary against the booking confirmations, open the final-month conversation from it, and move the seating plan and running order into artifacts and the standing documents into Project knowledge
Option CAsk Claude for a summary of the planning so far and paste it straight into a new conversation, since Claude wrote the summary from the full history and it is the most reliable record available
Option DKeep the single conversation going to the wedding day, since every decision lives in it, and a new conversation would lose three months of context
[Check Answer]

A requirement is a statement of what a piece of work must achieve. Use-case analysis is judging whether a task is a good candidate for Claude before you put any effort into it. A theme is a named group of related comments. The objective tests two related skills: using Claude to turn messy input into structured requirements, and use-case analysis. Every workflow decision in this domain starts with two questions: what does this work require, and does Claude belong in it at all? Both skills follow one rule: Claude structures, and the human validates and owns the result.

This lesson uses one made-up example throughout: a newsagent that runs home deliveries. The owner wants to rework her paper rounds. Her material is customer emails, staff meeting notes, order-book comments and remarks from the counter.

Real requirements arrive as complaint threads, meeting notes, survey comments and half-remembered conversations, never as a tidy list. The Help Center lists summarising long documents and conversations among Claude's core uses, alongside generating viewpoints and providing recommendations. Given the raw material, Claude clusters it into themes and separates what people asked for from what they appear to need. It also shows where two groups want incompatible things, and names what nobody mentioned.

For the newsagent, Claude might return themes like late papers and wrong magazines. It might flag that one estate wants papers before seven, while staff want later starts. The reading takes minutes instead of an afternoon, and the people involved get an outline of the problem that they can question.

Claude organises what you gave it. It has no way of knowing what your organisation needs. A theme that Claude names is a hypothesis about your input, not a finding about your business. The people whose requirements the theme describes must confirm it before anyone bases any design on it. Anthropic's AI Fluency framework divides the work in the same way. Discernment means evaluating what the AI produced. Diligence means staying accountable for the result. Both stay with the human.
So the owner checks the early-papers conflict with the estate's customers and her staff before she redraws any round. If she designed straight from Claude's themes, she would mistake tidy output for validated requirements. Confirming the themes is the cheap part.

h: The Shape of a Strong Candidate
t:
Good Claude use cases share some recognisable features:
The work is mainly about language: drafting, summarising, reformatting, explaining, comparing. These are the tasks that the Help Center's use-case article documents.
The material needed is material you can provide.
The output can be checked by someone competent to check it.
Either the volume is high or starting from nothing is the expensive part.

h: The Shape of a Strong Candidate
t:
AI Fluency calls this judgement Delegation: deciding what work to hand to the AI. It treats Delegation as a separate skill, and that skill comes before anyone writes any prompt. Weak candidates have the opposite features. The work needs the authority to decide rather than the ability to draft. Or it depends on information Claude has no access to. Or it is relationship work rather than document work.
At the newsagent, a letter announcing new delivery times is a strong candidate: the owner can check it. Choosing who takes which round needs authority. Knowing whether a paper reached a doorstep needs information Claude lacks. Calling the regular customer who cancelled is relationship work.

People skip one test in particular. It says: if you could not tell whether the answer was wrong, you are not ready to use Claude on that task. Without a checker, a wrong output passes as easily as a right one. High stakes are not a reason to abandon the work, and neither is a missing checker. Both mean that you find the person who can tell good output from bad output, and you put that person in the process.

The test also splits the blank-cheque use case. A blank-cheque use case is the announcement that Claude will handle a whole category of work. A category mixes strong and weak candidates. The commitment to the whole category comes before the analysis that should have decided its scope. Handing Claude all the delivery admin would group the letter with the choice of who takes which round.

The failure that the exam tests most often here is the skipped confirmation step. Whether and where the work suits Claude is this objective's question. How you then phrase the request is Domain 1's skill, and which product feature runs the work is Domain 3's skill.
[Key Concept] When a 4.1 question ends with themes that Claude has just clustered, the right answer acts before design begins. It returns the themes to the people who own the requirements. The wrong options adopt the themes as findings, hand Claude the decision itself, or abandon the work because the stakes feel high.

[Exam Trap] Adopting Claude's themes as validated findings because they arrived quickly and read plausibly
A theme is a hypothesis about the input, not a finding about the business. Basing a design on unconfirmed structure builds the wrong thing. Take the themes back to the people whose requirements they are, and confirm them before design begins.
[Exam Trap] Handing Claude the decision along with the analysis
Decisions that belong to an accountable person or group stay with them. Claude structures the material and drafts what supports the decision, but choosing the policy, picking the winner or resolving the dispute is theirs.
[Exam Trap] Excluding work from Claude as too important

Refusing to use Claude treats high stakes as if they were high risk. High stakes call for a competent checker in the process, not abandoning the drafting help. Without a checker, a wrong output passes as easily as a right one.

The manager of a Saturday street market has a folder of complaint emails and comments from traders about how pitches are allocated. She wants to establish what a fairer allocation approach must do before anyone designs one. Claude clusters the material into six themes, including a contradiction: regular traders believe casual traders get the best corner pitches, while casual traders describe those same corners as reserved for regulars. She has no time to work through the folder again herself. What should she do next?
Option ATreat the themes as hypotheses about her input and take them back to the traders to confirm, starting with the contradiction, before any design work begins

Option BSet the folder aside and re-read every email herself, since pitch allocation is too contentious for Claude to be involved at all
Option CHand the allocation question over entirely: give Claude the pitch map and the trader list and ask it to produce the fairest possible allocation for next season
Option DAdopt the six themes as the requirements document, since they come straight from the traders’ own words, and move on to designing the new allocation approach
[Check Answer]

Research gathers and synthesises outside material, so you start from material that already exists. Planning turns a goal into ordered steps. Process optimisation finds and fixes the step that slows a process. All three work the same way: Claude makes the first draft, and you make the decisions about it.
This lesson uses one made-up example throughout: an estate agency. Its manager uses Claude for all three: other agencies' valuation practice, an open-house weekend plan, and slow lettings.

The product supports research at two scales, and the Help Center describes the difference. Web search suits straightforward factual queries that one or two lookups can answer. Research mode runs multiple searches that build on each other. It explores different angles of a question and addresses the open questions systematically. It returns cited findings and suits bigger multi-source jobs. At the agency, one lettings rule is a job for web search. A survey of valuation practice is a job for Research.
The value is coverage and speed. The limit is that anything important gets checked before anyone repeats it, whether it has citations or not. A citation shows where a finding came from, not that the finding is right.

h: Plans Are Built from Stated Constraints
t: Starting from Claude's first plan is better than starting from nothing. Claude is good at finding gaps in a plan. If you ask what a plan is missing, you get dependencies, sequencing problems and the step that everyone forgets.

h: Plans Are Built from Stated Constraints
t: Claude will also confidently make plans that omit constraints you never mentioned, because it does not know them. Examples are the one accessible entrance, the volunteer who cannot work Sundays and the double-booked room. Nothing in the output warns you that Claude built the plan without them. An unconstrained open-house plan might staff Sunday viewings with a negotiator who never works Sundays. The plan is wrong, but it looks correct. That makes it more dangerous than an obviously bad plan, because people are more likely to trust it.

h: Plans Are Built from Stated Constraints
t: This is easy to prevent. Anthropic's business prompt-engineering guidance says to treat Claude like an intern on its first day, with clear, explicit instructions and all the necessary detail. For a useful plan, put the real constraints in the brief, then ask for the assumptions that the plan rests on. When the plan states an assumption, you can read it and correct it.

Claude generates hypotheses about where a process is slow, fragile or duplicated. It cannot tell you which one is true, because it has never watched your process run. Data decides which hypothesis is true. The loop has four steps:
Describe the process and its constraints.
Ask for candidate bottlenecks, and for the evidence that would confirm each one.
Collect that evidence.
Change the step that the evidence identifies.
Evidence comes after Claude names the hypotheses, so you know what you are looking for. Evidence comes before anything changes, so the change has a target. For the agency's lettings, Claude might suggest slow referencing or late landlord sign-off. The stage dates in the agency's own files decide between them.

The same guidance advises approaching the work like a scientist, and testing and iterating often. It also advises pairing prompt work with the organisation's own subject-matter experts rather than trusting either alone.

The most expensive mistake is optimising a step that was never the constraint. It wastes the budget on a step that was working, and people are then less willing to try another change. It usually comes from treating the most plausible hypothesis as the confirmed one. The cause that looks most likely is often the real one, so it is tempting to act without evidence. But the likely cause is wrong often enough to make this expensive. Collecting the evidence that shows the real cause usually needs a day's work. Suppose the dates show that landlord sign-off causes the delay. If the agency buys faster referencing, it spends its money and the delay remains.

The exam tests your judgement, not Claude's first draft. Every right answer in this objective either supplies the facts Claude could not know or checks something before acting. Every wrong option that recurs treats a fluent output as a finished one. Domain 3 covers which feature does the research. This objective tests the practice around that feature. Checking findings before repeating them belongs to Domain 2.
How to spot the right answer
In this objective's questions, the right answer checks the evidence before changing anything: last season's timings, the usage records, the complaint log. The wrong options redesign the process based on reasoning that sounds convincing, or choose a bigger feature when local facts were missing.

[Exam Trap] Treating a plausible, well-structured plan as a checked one
Claude confidently makes plans that ignore constraints it was not told, and nothing in the output warns you. The plan looks correct but is wrong. Put the real constraints in the brief, then ask for the assumptions it is based on.
[Exam Trap] Changing the process because of the best-sounding hypothesis
Claude's candidate bottlenecks are hypotheses; it has never watched the process run. Acting on the most plausible one can spend money on a step that was fine. Get the evidence that would confirm each one, then change the step that the evidence identifies.
[Exam Trap] Substituting more research for local evidence

Citations from elsewhere cannot say which cause is true in your process. Research mode suits bigger multi-source jobs, but the deciding evidence here is the process's own data. Pull that data before changing anything.

A city bike-hire scheme's coordinator keeps hearing that commuter-belt docking stations are empty by eight in the morning. She describes the scheme to Claude, which suggests four plausible causes: the overnight rebalancing round finishes too early, two residential stations feed the same office cluster, weekend maintenance keeps bikes off the road on Mondays, and riders arriving at full stations cycle on with the bikes. Only her own scheme's figures will show which cause is the real one, and she will act on none of them until they do. What is the professional next step?
Option AAdd a second morning rebalancing round straight away, since the first cause Claude listed is the most plausible one and the mornings are when the complaints arrive

Option BAsk Claude what evidence would confirm or rule out each cause, then pull the scheme’s trip and docking data before changing anything at all
Option CRun the same question again in Research mode so that the four candidate causes come back supported by citations from other cities’ bike schemes
Option DAsk Claude to redesign the docking network around commuter flows, treating the empty morning stations as sufficient evidence that the current layout has failed
[Check Answer]

Solution iteration means improving a deliverable over several rounds, with Claude as the drafting partner. In this certification a solution is a process, a template, a piece of guidance, a scheme, a service design, a form or a plan. It is never software. Each round is checked against a criterion: a test drawn from the requirement established in 4.1.
This lesson uses one made-up example throughout: a coffee shop whose owner wants a Saturday opening checklist for one barista working alone. The requirement says who the checklist is for and which problems it must handle, such as a late milk delivery. Claude's first draft is workable.

h: Why the Loop Is Worth Running
t: Iteration used to be expensive, so people defended their first draft. The cost of an alternative was the reason not to look at one. Claude changes this cost. A second and third version cost minutes, so you can afford to look at them. Comparing three concrete options is a better way to design than arguing about one. The owner's question changes from whether the checklist is good to which version meets the requirement. This change of question is the purpose of this objective. The change only works while the versions stay disposable. You can discard a cheap draft with no formality, and you can honestly test a version that nobody personally prefers.

Every round needs a named criterion from the requirement. The named criterion separates iteration from random small changes. "Make it better" produces something different, not something better. Without new information, the revision has no target. For the same reason, the Help Center's remedy for an unhelpful answer is specific feedback rather than a plain retry. "Make this survive a wet day" is a testable change.

Run each round against one criterion. Check the result against that criterion alone. Keep the version that passes. The owner asks for a checklist that still works when the milk delivery is late, then checks only that. You can rank two versions that you judge against the same test. When people judge two versions on overall feel, they just argue about them. Anthropic's AI Fluency course names this cycle the Description-Discernment Loop: describe what you need, evaluate what Claude returned, refine, and repeat.

Stop when the remaining changes are matters of preference rather than fitness (how well the deliverable meets the requirement). Polishing a deliverable that already meets the requirement uses time that the next problem needed. Polishing also risks a subtler failure: a fluent, confident version can replace the one that your actual users needed. So check against the requirement and the users, never against how the prose reads.

If a round shows that the requirement itself was wrong, the next step is to revisit the requirement, not to write another draft. No revision fixes a deliverable that is built for the wrong requirement. Suppose the owner learns that two staff open on Saturdays. The requirement needs rewriting before any further draft. Whichever way the loop ends, state the stopping reason in one line. Naming the reason keeps the loop honest the next time it runs.

In the product, this loop uses artifacts. Substantial, standalone content appears in its own dedicated window. You revise the artifact by asking Claude to change it. To compare two concrete options, edit the message that produced the draft. The edit creates a different version of the chat, called a branch. The new branch has its own artifacts. The original branch keeps the first draft intact. The owner gets a second checklist without losing the first. Comparing two branches is better than trusting your memory of the round before, because memory makes whichever version came last seem better. Keep the requirement visible while you compare. The branches show the versions, but only the requirement says which version is better.

Candidates most often confuse this objective with Domain 1. Iterating the prompt to get a better response is Domain 1.3. Iterating the solution, with Claude as the drafting partner, is 4.3: the same loop, run on a different object.
[Key Concept] When a 4.3 question shows a workable first draft, the right answer names one criterion drawn from the requirement and checks the revision against it. Wrong options make changes without a criterion, generate many drafts and pick the one that feels best, or put an untested draft into live use. When the question signals that the requirement itself is wrong, the right answer revisits the requirement.

[Exam Trap] Round after round of asking Claude to make it better with no named criterion
Each round produces a different version, none of them checkably better, because no criterion directs the revision. Name one criterion drawn from the requirement and test the result against it.
[Exam Trap] Redrafting a deliverable whose requirement was wrong
No amount of revision fixes a deliverable built for the wrong requirement. When a round shows the requirement itself has failed, go back to the requirement from 4.1 and rework it before any further draft.
[Exam Trap] Letting the best-written version replace the one that meets the requirement

A well-written version does not always meet the requirement. Versions are checked against the requirement and the users, not against each other's prose, and the warm, confident draft that misses a hard constraint is precisely the version the exam expects you to reject.

The party coordinator at a laser-tag arena is designing the running order for a new birthday-party package. The requirement is fixed: ages seven to eleven, a safety briefing before anyone plays, food in the party room, all inside a ninety-minute slot. Claude's first draft is workable. She wants round two to give her a version she can plainly pass or fail, before any real party relies on it. What should round two look like?
Option AUse the draft at this weekend’s parties exactly as written, treating the live sessions as the test round and adjusting it afterwards
Option BAsk Claude to make the running order more fun and more polished, and keep regenerating until a version feels right

Option CStart a fresh chat for each draft and collect five alternative running orders, then choose whichever of the five reads best overall
Option DRevise against one named criterion, say handling a party that arrives fifteen minutes late, and check the result against that criterion alone
[Check Answer]

In this certification, integration is about two questions. Where in an existing process does a person bring work to Claude? Does the process stay the same? Integration never means a technical connection between systems. To augment is to give Claude one slow step. To redesign is to change the process itself. To escalate is to pass work beyond the Associate's role to someone else.
This lesson uses one made-up example throughout: a dry cleaner. Every Monday its manager prepares a write-up of last week's damage claims. Customers who leave garments uncollected get a reminder letter.

When Claude does the slow step, everything else stays the same. The write-up takes ten minutes instead of an hour. The manager still owns the write-up, and nobody else's job changes. So augmentation is cheap, reversible and easy to explain to colleagues. If augmentation fails, the manager does the write-up by hand again. Augmentation is the right choice far more often than the ambitious alternative. Most successful integrations for an Associate improve one step.

In a redesign the process changes because the constraint that decided how the process works has gone. Personalising a reminder letter used to cost twenty minutes, so the dry cleaner sent one generic letter. When a personalised letter costs two minutes, a tiered approach that nobody would have proposed becomes possible.

Redesign is rarer and bigger, so a redesign gets a pilot before a rollout. Anthropic's enterprise deployment guidance stages adoption this way. A pilot group is monitored for feedback over a period of weeks before wider expansion. Champions are identified per team. The dry cleaner tries tiered letters on one batch first. An all-at-once rollout measures nothing. It leaves nothing to compare against, and it risks everything at once.

Find the step where the decision happens. Keep a person on that step. Integrations fail when the checking step is removed. Checking has no visible output, so it looks like waste to anyone redesigning from a diagram. The dry cleaner's manager signs each letter before the letter is sent. This signing step is the human gate. The gate also makes augmentation safe to adopt quickly. The person who always signed the letters still signs them, so a person still makes the judgement in the process.

Some requests are outside this role because they need a technical implementation. A technical implementation means systems that communicate with each other, data that moves on its own, or a process built to run with nobody present. Suppose the owner wants reminders sent overnight, straight from the till system. That request means connecting the till system to whatever sends the letters. This connection is technical work. The professional action is to escalate the request to a Claude Developer or Architect, with a clear written description of what the process needs. Describing the need well is itself the Associate's contribution. Escalation is no failure. Escalation shows that you know the limits of your own job.

Connectors let Claude retrieve data and take actions in connected services. Connectors operate inside a conversation, when a person's requests need them. The Google Workspace documentation states that Claude only accesses your data when you explicitly ask a question or request an action requiring it. The features this exam covers include chat, Projects, research, artifacts and connectors. Within these features, work starts when a person asks for it.

Current state (checked 14 October 2026): Claude Cowork, which the exam guide does not name, has scheduled tasks. Anthropic's Cowork course says a task that only uses your connectors can run remotely at its set time. On the exam, the Associate still escalates a request for work that runs by itself. This is because the exam treats such a request as a technical implementation beyond this role.

Recurring work belongs in a Project, not in one conversation that grows longer and longer. A Project is a self-contained workspace with its own chat histories and knowledge. When a chat approaches its length limit, the Help Center advises starting a new conversation or using a Project. The manager keeps the Monday write-up in a Project. Where a plan supports sharing, a Project gives a team one shared environment for its documents and instructions. Chats inside a Project are not shared by default. A member sees the Project's contents, knowledge and instructions. Each person's own conversations stay private unless they choose to share one. This objective is about deciding that the work belongs in a Project. Domain 5 is about configuring the Project and maintaining its instructions and knowledge.

If you know the meaning of integration, you can answer many questions. The wrong options are usually integrations in the technical sense. The right answer is an integration in this lesson's sense. Learn the words in a question that signal a technical implementation, which needs an escalation: automatically, without anyone having to, straight from the system, overnight.
Proposing full automation

Connecting Claude to a system, or configuring Claude to run unattended, is this domain's typical wrong option. It is never the right answer. Escalate because the request is a technical implementation, beyond this role and the features this exam covers. Never base the escalation on a claim that no Claude product could run the work. Cowork's scheduled tasks can run some tasks at a set time. The exam guide does not name these scheduled tasks.

[Exam Trap] Improvising an unattended pipeline that connects systems together
Systems connected together, auto-publishing and unattended pipelines are technical implementations, beyond the Associate's role and the features this exam covers. Improvised versions fail silently with nobody present to catch them. The professional action is a clear escalation brief to a Claude Developer or Architect.
[Exam Trap] Redesigning the whole process at once
The all-at-once rollout means that if it fails, everything fails together and nothing was learned. A redesign needs a pilot on one part of the process first, with a measurement, exactly as Anthropic's own deployment guidance stages adoption.
[Exam Trap] Removing the checking step to save time

The human gate produces no visible output, which makes it look like waste on a process diagram. It is the step where a person makes the process's judgement, so keep the person on the deciding step and check each output before it goes out.

A local newspaper's events page is compiled every week by an editorial assistant from event details that venues email in. A colleague proposes that Claude should instead gather the listings from the venues' websites overnight and publish the finished page without anyone touching it. The assistant still wants to save time on this week's page, with a person reading every listing before it runs. How should the assistant respond?
Option AAgree, and spend the week experimenting with connectors until Claude can collect the venue listings and produce the page each night with nobody involved
Option BDecline any use of Claude on the page at all, since a listing with one wrong date or time would damage the paper’s credibility with readers and venues

Option CEscalate the overnight version to the technical team with a note of what the process needs, meanwhile using Claude to reformat the emailed submissions for checking
Option DRedesign the whole listings operation all at once: print, web and social editions built from the same submitted material and launched together
[Check Answer]

A stakeholder here is a colleague who reads your report on a Claude trial and decides what happens next. Reporting to them has one rule: say what is true, including the parts that are not impressive. The rule serves two audiences: the enthusiast and the sceptic.
This lesson uses one made-up example throughout: a tyre fitter whose office manager is reporting on a three-month Claude trial. Here, accuracy is a useful tactic as well as a form of modesty. If she over-promises, she wins a mandate that she cannot deliver. Then stakeholders read the first visible error as proof that the whole trial was oversold. If she under-claims, the work does not get the support that it earned. A sceptic cannot disprove an accurate claim.

State value in four parts: the task, the before, the after, and how you know. "The monthly board pack takes two hours instead of five, measured across three months" is a claim the tyre fitter's manager can defend. "Claude has transformed how we work" is not a claim: it names no task and no measurement, so nobody can check it. An audience that has heard that sentence before will discount everything that follows it.
Anthropic's enterprise guidance says the same. Productivity gains, such as hours saved, are measured through periodic user surveys. The gains are reported to stakeholders at regular intervals. The guidance pairs quantitative data with qualitative examples, in place of enthusiasm.

Every figure in the report appears because somebody measured it over a stated period, never because it sounds about right. A measured saving applies to its own task. The report never projects the board pack figure onto work that the trial did not include.

State limitations plainly: what still needs a person and why, what went wrong during the pilot, and what has not been tested. People omit the untested category. This gap causes trouble later, because stakeholders take the lack of a statement as a claim. If a stakeholder is never told that some work went untrialled, the stakeholder will reasonably assume that the trial covered that work. The eventual failure is then blamed on the report that said nothing about it, as well as on the work. If the tyre fitter never tried Claude on warranty claims, naming that gap costs one sentence. If the report leaves the gap unnamed, the report loses its credibility when the gap becomes visible.

A caught error is evidence for the process. Suppose a booking confirmation used the wrong date and the read-through caught the error. When you report the error, a sceptic learns that the checking step works. This is the very thing that the sceptic doubted. If the report hides the error and the error becomes visible later, readers re-read every other claim in the report as selected to look good. Reporting a caught error is the Diligence element of AI Fluency in reporting form. Diligence means that you stay accountable for what the AI produced, including in what you tell colleagues about it.

Stakeholders have one of two attitudes, and each attitude needs something different from the same truthful account. The enthusiast, perhaps the tyre fitter's owner, wants Claude in use across the whole business by Friday. The enthusiast needs to hear the limitations and the human gate without losing the enthusiasm that will make the work progress. So the answer to "can it handle all of it now?" is not a plain no: the answer names what stays human. The sceptic, perhaps a fitter, suspects that Claude is a useless novelty, a risk or a threat to somebody's job. The sceptic needs the measured result, the named human step, and an honest account of what went wrong and how it was caught.

Overcorrection fails with both audiences. Overcorrection means so many caveats that a working result sounds like a failure. Under-claiming is not honesty. It gives the sceptic a conclusion that the data does not support.

A prepared candidate treats a caught error as evidence. Whether a use is permitted, and who must approve it, belongs to Domain 6. This objective covers the honest account of results to colleagues, never a governance sign-off.
Use only measured numbers
In this objective's questions, the only number that can support the right answer is one that the question itself says was measured. Any option that quotes a saving that nobody measured, or that projects a measured saving onto untested work, is wrong. The option is wrong however reasonable the figure sounds.

[Exam Trap] Presenting enthusiasm as evidence
A transformation claim with no task, no before, no after and no measurement cannot be checked. So a sceptical audience discounts it. The audience also discounts the genuinely measured result underneath it. A defensible claim states the four parts and stops.
[Exam Trap] Projecting a measured saving onto untested work
A measured result belongs to the task it was measured on. Extending it to a category the trial never included quotes a number nobody measured, and the exam treats it as wrong regardless of how plausible the projection looks.
[Exam Trap] Leaving the pilot's caught error out of the report

When the error becomes visible later, every other claim gets re-read as selected to look good. Disclosed, the same error was evidence that the checking step works, which is exactly what the sceptical audience needed to hear.
[Exam Trap] Hiding a working result among many caveats
So many warnings make a working process sound like one that failed, handing the sceptic a conclusion the data does not support. State the measured result and its period plainly, keep the limits the trial found and name what it never tested.

The coordinator of a talking newspaper for blind and partially sighted listeners has trialled Claude for three months. Listener letters now reach a first draft in minutes rather than half an hour, measured across the trial, with every letter still read and approved by a volunteer before it goes out. Edition scripts saw no saving, because the recording sessions were always the bottleneck. One draft gave the wrong date for the annual listeners' tea and was caught at the read-through. The committee has asked for what the trial showed, with nothing projected or hypothetical and nothing left out. What should the report to the management committee say?

Option ALead with the correspondence saving and leave out the wrong date, since one caught slip would only give the committee a reason to stop a trial that is clearly working well
Option BOpen with the risks: list every possible failure before mentioning the saving, so nobody on the committee can later accuse the coordinator of having over-sold the trial
Option CRecommend extending Claude to the edition scripts as well, projecting a saving on the scripts similar to the one already measured on the listener letters
Option DReport all three findings to the committee exactly as they stand, presenting the caught date for the annual tea as evidence that the volunteer read-through does its job
[Check Answer]

Anthropic's Help Center describes a Project as a self-contained workspace with its own chat histories and knowledge base. A Project has two configurable halves. The Help Center documents them separately because they do different work. Custom instructions are where you set how Claude should behave and respond. They tailor Claude's responses: for example, a more formal tone, or answers from the perspective of a specific role or industry. Project knowledge is the material Claude works from. You upload relevant documents, text and files to the knowledge base. Claude uses them to understand the context and background of chats in the Project. Instructions answer "how should this work be done?" Knowledge answers "what should it be done from?"

This lesson uses one made-up example throughout: a window cleaning firm whose manager writes quotes and reminders every week. Each time, she tells Claude to write to homeowners in plain words and give the next visit date. Each time, she attaches the price list, the terms of service and good past replies. Both halves are ordinary setup steps in the Project screen: write and save the instructions, then use the add button to upload the knowledge files.

Configuring a Project well depends on one sorting decision, which you apply to each piece in turn. Is this a rule about behaviour, or material to consult? For the window cleaning firm, "write to homeowners in plain words" is behaviour, so it belongs in the instructions. The price list is material, so it belongs in the knowledge.
The test matters because each container has properties the other lacks. Claude applies the instructions to every chat in the Project. Claude consults knowledge when the work needs it. You can replace a knowledge file in one step when the document is revised. You have to find a policy that is pasted into the instructions and remove it by hand.

The first failure is reference material pasted into the instructions. The usual reason given is thoroughness: put the whole policy where Claude can never miss it. Then the pasted content hides the behavioural rules. When the policy is revised, the stale text stays in a place where you cannot cleanly replace it. If you paste the firm's terms of service into the instructions, the two behavioural rules then sit inside pages of terms.

The second failure is the reverse: a rule placed in the knowledge base. A house style guide uploaded as a document is material about behaviour, not an instruction. Nothing marks the style guide as a rule for every response, so the style guide is applied only when the Project happens to consult it. If the firm uploaded its style guide as knowledge, the style guide would apply only some of the time. A rule that is applied only some of the time is not a standard. A rule that the work depends on every time belongs in the instructions, stated as a behaviour.

h: Build the Setup from What You Already Do
t: The method needs no fresh analysis, because anyone doing the work by hand already has both lists. Whatever you re-explain at the start of every conversation is the instruction set: the audience, the tone, the format, the standing rules. Whatever you re-attach is the knowledge base: the policies, the templates, the past examples. At the window cleaning firm, the two rules become instructions and the three files become knowledge. Write the first list as behaviours and upload the second as files. Then run the next real task with a short task-only prompt, and note what you no longer had to say.

This objective starts after the Project decision and tests how well you configure the Project. Whether a piece of work deserves a Project at all is Domain 3's judgement. Where a Project sits in a wider process is Domain 4's. Most questions here are a scenario that asks you to sort each piece as behaviour or material, which is the container test, so practise the test until it is automatic. Both wrong-container failures are common in real setups and make effective wrong options. Because the question begins after that decision, "use a Project" is never the right answer here. An option that argues that decision again belongs to Domain 3.

[Key Concept] When an exam question offers competing setups, apply the container test to each piece the question mentions. The right answer puts behaviour in the instructions and material in the knowledge. The wrong options put at least one piece in the other container, usually presented as thoroughness or tidiness.

[Exam Trap] Pasting the reference document into the custom instructions so Claude can never miss it
Pasted reference text hides the behavioural rules. When the document is revised, the old text has to be found and cut out by hand, whereas a knowledge file can be replaced in one step. Keep the rules in the instructions.
[Exam Trap] Uploading the standing rule as a knowledge document and expecting it to govern every response
Knowledge is material Claude consults, not standing behaviour. A rule that must hold every time gets applied only sometimes unless it is stated in the instructions, which is the job instructions exist to do.

[Exam Trap] Skipping the Project and re-explaining and re-attaching everything in each chat, presented as keeping things current
Keeping material current is handled by swapping the knowledge file when the source document changes. The per-chat workaround re-introduces the exact overhead the Project removes, and it depends on every user remembering to do it.

The secretary of a tenants and residents association has decided the estate casework and the monthly meeting papers belong in one Project and is now setting it up. Two pieces are in hand: the association repairs policy, and the rule that every letter must name the responsible officer and the date the repair was reported. Where should each go?
Option AUpload the repairs policy to the project knowledge, and write the rule about naming the responsible officer and the report date into the custom instructions
Option BPaste the repairs policy into the custom instructions so Claude can never overlook it, and upload a short guidance note that mentions the responsible-officer rule to the project knowledge

Option CUpload both the repairs policy and a document stating the responsible-officer rule as knowledge files, and leave the custom instructions empty so the Project stays flexible
Option DKeep both out of the Project and re-attach the policy and restate the rule at the start of each new chat, since freshly pasted material is always the current version
[Check Answer]

A Project's knowledge is the material that Claude uses inside that Project. The material reaches the Project by one of two routes. An upload puts a copy into the Project's knowledge base: documents, text, code and other files. A connector links Claude to the live source, such as Google Drive. Each route has properties the other lacks. The choice of route depends on how the material changes.
This lesson uses one made-up example throughout: a painter and decorator who creates a Project for quoting and job planning. The decorator's terms and conditions and method statement barely change. The job schedule is a Google Doc in Drive. It changes every week.

h: A Snapshot or the Live Source
t: An uploaded file is a copy taken on the day of upload. Every user of the Project sees the same copy, so it is stable and predictable. When the source is superseded, the copy stays as it was. Nothing tells you that the source was superseded. The copy looks as current in six months as on the day of upload. This stable copy suits the terms and conditions. It does not suit the job schedule, because a copy of the schedule would be wrong within a week.

h: A Snapshot or the Live Source
t: A connector suits material that changes, because the connector reaches the live source when you ask. The Google Workspace documentation states that Google Docs added to chats and projects sync directly from Google Drive. It says that, as a result, you are always working with the latest version. The documentation also states that Claude only accesses your data when you explicitly ask a question or request an action that requires it. It states that Claude then retrieves the minimum information needed.

h: A Snapshot or the Live Source
t: The latest version includes a colleague's half-finished edit at the moment of your question. If the office manager is halfway through moving Tuesday's jobs, Claude reads them half moved. Live material includes unfinished changes like this, so it is often better to upload stable reference documents.

Not every workplace lets each person enable connectors for themselves. On Team and Enterprise plans, an Owner or Primary Owner needs to enable connectors for the organisation before members can use them. If connectors are off in your workspace, the right step is to ask whoever administers the workspace, not to improvise.
Through a connector, each person has the same access that they already have in the connected service. If someone cannot access a file in the source system, the connector cannot access it from Claude either. Two colleagues using the same Project can get different answers from the same connector. This difference is a property of the permission system, not a fault in the Project.

Connectors are not read-only. They can retrieve data and take actions in connected services. The Gmail connector can send, reply to and forward email from your own account. By default Claude asks for your approval before each of these actions. The decorator still approves each quote email before Claude sends it.

When a Project has a substantial knowledge base, Claude does not read all of it on every question. The documentation describes how Claude searches project knowledge and loads only the most relevant content. This search, called retrieval, activates as a project approaches or exceeds the limits of its context window. Retrieval has to find the right document among all the material that you supplied.
Two documented steps help. Clear, descriptive file names help retrieval find the right material. For example, "terms-and-conditions" is a better name than "final-v2-new". You can also name a specific document in your prompt to focus the search on it.

A Project's knowledge is not an archive. Every document that is never needed adds unneeded material to the search space, which is the material that Claude searches. Such a document also gives Claude a chance to quote it at the wrong moment. A small set of relevant documents is better than a bulk upload. Remove files that are no longer in active use, rather than keeping them.

When you receive a shared drive, pick the few documents that the work needs. Route each document by how it changes. Route material that changes, such as the decorator's job schedule, through a connector to its live source. Upload stable reference material, such as the method statement. A colleague who wants you to add everything to the Project means well. The cost appears later, as answers based on the wrong document.

Exam questions test whether you match the route to the material. In almost every question, the clue is how the material changes. Domain 6 asks whether a document is permitted in the Project at all, on privacy, contractual or policy grounds. This objective is about managing material that is already allowed in the Project.
Current state: where the Drive route is available

The exam guide names Google Drive as a connector to manage alongside uploads. The right answer routes material that changes through the Drive connector. As of 28 September 2026, the Google Workspace connectors article describes the Drive route as adding one document at a time. The article describes adding documents only to a private Project's Files. You add each one by searching your recent documents or pasting its link. The article says the option is disabled for shared Projects. The Files of a shared Project accept uploads. The connector still works in chats: Google Docs added to a chat sync directly from Drive. On the exam, route by how the material changes.
What to notice in the exam

The right answer to an upload-or-connector question depends on how the material changes, never on how important the material is. Route the weekly job schedule through the connector, however trivial it looks. Upload the terms and conditions, which barely change, however important they are.

[Exam Trap] Bringing in the whole shared drive so nothing is missing
The dump reads as diligence and is the posture curation exists to correct. Retrieval must find the right document among everything supplied, so every irrelevant file makes the relevant one harder to surface and more likely to be displaced by a wrong-moment quote.
[Exam Trap] Choosing between upload and connector by how important the material is
An upload is a snapshot that goes stale silently, however important it is. Frequently revised material suits a connector, stable material an upload. Current docs (October 2026) say the Drive route works only for private Projects, so a shared Project takes a dated upload.

[Exam Trap] Having a Team-plan user switch on an organisation connector themselves
An Owner or Primary Owner must enable connectors for the organisation before members can use them, so the right step is to ask the workspace administrator. Options in which the candidate tries to enable connectors personally are testing exactly this governance step.

A show cave preservation society is setting up the knowledge for a Project covering guide rotas, opening arrangements and volunteer communications. The guide rota and the opening times, which change with the water level after rain, live in a shared Drive folder; the constitution, the site risk assessments and the guide handbook barely change. A trustee suggests bringing in the entire shared drive so everything is available. Material unrelated to those three areas should not be in the Project. What is the best setup?
Option AUpload everything as files, including the current rota and opening times, so every user of the Project sees exactly the same stable set of documents whenever they ask

Option BBring in the entire shared drive as the trustee suggests, so every document the society holds, from committee minutes to old correspondence, is available to the Project from day one without anyone having to choose
Option CKeep knowledge out of the Project, and have whoever is asking paste the current rota and opening times into their chat each time
Option DAdd the rota and the opening times from Drive so chats work from the current versions, upload the constitution, risk assessments and handbook as files, and leave the rest of the drive out
[Check Answer]

In this certification, system-level instructions means the standing rules a person writes in plain English. These rules are in one of three places: the claude.ai settings, a Project, or, for an administrator, the organisation settings. There is no technical layer underneath.
This lesson uses one made-up example throughout: a small locksmith firm. Its office manager uses Claude for customer emails, landlord quotes and home-security guides. Some of her rules are true of her. Some are true of the quotes, some are true of everyone at the firm, and some are true only of this week. Two choices decide whether those rules work: where she places each rule, and how she words it.

Each level has an owner and a reach (the conversations it applies to), and all three are documented.
Account-wide. The claude.ai settings have a box labelled Instructions, under Settings > Your Claude (Instructions for Claude in the older Settings layout). Anything written there applies to all of your conversations. The suggested content is personal and applies across all your work, such as preferred approaches, common terms and general communication preferences.
Project-level. Instructions defined for a Project tailor Claude's responses in that Project's chats only.

Organisation-level. On Team and Enterprise plans, Owners and Primary Owners can set organisation instructions. Claude follows them in every conversation across the organisation.
Where levels overlap, organisation instructions take precedence. Individual instructions still apply to anything the organisation instructions do not address. An Owner's rule on email sign-offs takes precedence over her own rule on sign-offs. Her spelling rule still applies, because the organisation set nothing on spelling.

The practical point is about role, not mechanics. An ordinary member does not set organisation instructions. So if a rule should bind the whole organisation, a member asks whoever administers the workspace to add it. If she wants every colleague's drafts to omit customers' home addresses, she asks the Owner to add that rule.

Place every rule by asking what it is true of. A rule applies to every chat at its level, so the level should match that answer.
True of you across all your work, such as your language, a summary first, or a non-specialist audience by default: account-wide.
True of one body of work, its audience, its format conventions, its standing rules: that Project's instructions.
True of everyone in the organisation: an organisation instruction, requested through the workspace Owner.
Only true of today's job: not an instruction at any level, but part of today's prompt.

Her British spelling and her rule to put the summary first are true of all her work, so they belong in the account-wide instructions. "Show the call-out fee as its own line" is true of the landlord quotes, so it belongs in that Project's instructions. This week's price rise belongs in this week's prompts.
A rule at the wrong level causes problems whether the level is too wide or too narrow. A Project rule moved to account level changes every unrelated conversation. Her call-out-fee rule would appear in the security guides. A rule that belongs everywhere but stays at Project level has to be copied and maintained in every Project that needs it. Her spelling rule would need a copy in every Project.

A useful instruction is checkable: someone could see whether it was followed. "Keep each item under ninety seconds when read aloud" can be followed and can be failed. Claude cannot follow "Be engaging" in any way that differs from how the work would have gone anyway. That instruction names no behaviour, so there is nothing to check.
The working test for every line: could a new colleague follow this and produce what you wanted? If not, the line says what you hope for, but it is not an instruction yet. "Sound trustworthy" fails the test for her quotes. "Put the price and the call-out fee in the first two lines" passes. Aspirations also make the set longer and make it look as if it covers more than it does.

h: Short and Prioritised Beats Long and Exhaustive
t: Standing instructions apply to every chat in their scope, so they should contain only what is true every time. A rule that is true of only one job distorts the other jobs. An instruction set that collects per-task detail stops describing the work. It starts to describe whichever task came last. If you put the price-rise note in the quotes Project, every later quote mentions it until someone removes it.

h: Short and Prioritised Beats Long and Exhaustive
t:
Length works the same way. Claude follows a short prioritised set more reliably than a long exhaustive one. When everything is a rule, Claude cannot follow every rule equally well. The rules that Claude follows less well are not the ones you would have chosen. When a set becomes too long for a colleague to remember, group it and prioritise it. Appending another rule does not fix it. Her quotes Project might group its rules under price, wording and layout, with price first.
Styles are a separate control that sets how a response is formatted and delivered (see the note below). Our reading of that is that Styles are not the place for rules about content.

This objective tests those two judgements: the level a rule is true of, and wording that can be checked. The point about role matches Domain 4: escalate, do not improvise. The line between a standing instruction and today's prompt is the cleanest boundary with Domain 1. Aspirations are the typical wrong option in this objective, because "tell it to be clear and professional" always reads as sensible advice.
[Key Concept] Two tests settle almost every question in this objective. Who or what does this rule apply to? The answer sets the level. Could a new colleague follow it and be checked against it? The answer sets the wording. The right answer passes both tests. Each wrong option fails exactly one.

The Help Center covered Styles only in one formatting comparison, so the point about substance is our reading, not a documented statement. Current state (checked 30 September 2026): the personalisation article no longer mentions Styles. Its formatting comparison names Skills for customising how Claude formats and delivers responses.

[Exam Trap] An aspiration written as an instruction: be professional, be thorough, produce high-quality work
Aspirations cannot be followed differently from the default and cannot be failed, so they change nothing and make the useful rules harder to follow. A checkable behaviour gives a new colleague something to follow and be checked against.
[Exam Trap] Writing this week's requirement into the standing instructions
A standing instruction applies to every chat in its scope. A rule true of one job distorts every other job until someone remembers to remove it; it belongs in that job's prompt, which is where the Domain 1 boundary sits.

[Exam Trap] Placing one Project's rules at account level, or setting an organisation-wide rule personally as an ordinary member
Account-wide rules change every unrelated conversation. Organisation instructions are set by Owners and Primary Owners on Team and Enterprise plans. So an ordinary member asks whoever administers the workspace. An Owner sets the rule directly.

An easy-read editor at a learning-disability self-advocacy charity is writing the Project instructions for the easy-read document summaries the charity produces for its members. Every line must still hold for documents produced years from now. Which instruction set will a volunteer checking the outputs be able to use?
Option AUse the sentence-length and everyday-word rules, plus a standing line to always include the closing date of the current member survey, because it matters to members right now
Option BBe clear, respectful and accessible at all times, and always produce high-quality easy-read documents that members of the charity will find genuinely useful

Option CKeep sentences under fifteen words with one idea each, use everyday words, explain any difficult word in brackets on first use, and end each summary by saying what the reader can do next
Option DPut the sentence-length and everyday-word rules in her account-wide Instructions for Claude rather than the Project, so every conversation she has follows the easy-read rules
[Check Answer]

A configuration is the setup of a Project: its custom instructions and its knowledge base. Claude applies the instructions to every chat within the Project. Claude also uses anything uploaded to the knowledge base in every chat within the Project. Keeping a configuration right has three duties: inform, maintain and update. The work has three parts: check on a schedule, remove old items rather than keep adding new ones, and remember the people that the configuration serves.
This lesson uses one made-up example throughout: a pet shop that configured a Project well last year to answer customer questions. Its knowledge base holds the price list and the returns policy. Nobody has changed the Project since.

h: Three Ways a Good Setup Decays
t:
Knowledge becomes out of date. An uploaded file is a copy from one moment, and nothing tells you that its source was superseded. Outputs continue to quote the old policy, price or procedure with complete confidence. At the pet shop, last year's price list still answers price questions.
Instructions become out of date. They apply to every chat, whether or not the situation they describe still exists. When the audience or the format changes, the rules continue to enforce the old situation.
The scope grows. When a Project works, people start to use it for related work. With each new task, the instructions written for the original job fit the work less well, until they fit none of the work.

h: Three Ways a Good Setup Decays
t: All three problems are invisible while you use the Project, so you have to schedule maintenance. If you wait for a sign that maintenance is needed, that sign never comes.

When a document is superseded, remove the old version. Do not add the new one alongside it. Completeness is a good quality in an archive. A working Project needs exactly one answer to which version is current. If a knowledge base holds both versions, Claude has no way to know which version is current.
