The pet shop uploads the new price list and deletes the old one.
Two compromise options fail: a note file explaining which version governs, or an instruction telling Claude to prefer the newer document. Both options compensate for a problem that the knowledge base should simply not have.

After you replace a document, also read the instructions for rules written for the old wording. A standing rule that quotes the old notice period stays after its source file is gone. At the pet shop, that rule might quote last year's returns window.

When colleagues share a Project, an unannounced change produces outputs that they cannot explain. They stop trusting those outputs. The person who made the change is rarely present when this happens.
The documentation gives one notification fact: members receive an email notification when a project is first shared with them. The documentation describes no notification of any kind for later edits to knowledge or instructions. So telling collaborators what changed and when is always a human step.

The date matters as much as the change, because it lets people tell whether work in progress was done before or after the change. People can recognise a reply drafted last week as pre-revision, instead of arguing about it. The pet shop's manager tells staff which file changed and on what day. Where a plan supports shared editing, several people may hold edit permission on the same Project. This makes it more important to say what changed.

The habit that works has three parts.
First, a named owner. "Someone should keep this current" means nobody does. A Project that has slowly gone out of date usually has no owner. The pet shop names its manager as owner.
Second, a review point tied to a real recurring event: the quarterly figures, the policy refresh, the start of the season. A diary note attached to something that already happens makes the review happen. A general intention does not. The pet shop reviews its Project whenever a new price list arrives.
Third, treat removal as an active step of the review. Additions happen naturally all year. Deletions happen only when someone asks which items are superseded and which have never been used.

The guide names the three duties. Every exam version of this objective is the same Project: a Project that was configured well once and has drifted since. Update matters least, because updating is easy once you have noticed. The guide names Inform explicitly, and almost everyone skips it.
Two boundaries apply. A question that opens with a bad output and asks what went wrong belongs to Domain 7. A perfectly maintained Project still produces first drafts whose facts get verified under Domain 2.
The additive trap

The wrong option that keeps both versions feels thorough and careful. This feeling is why the option is wrong: it treats a working tool as if it were an archive. The right answer removes the superseded version, checks the instructions, and tells the people who use the Project.

No Anthropic article covers editing a saved configuration or telling collaborators it changed. This lesson is based on the exam guide's objective wording, ordinary professional practice and the one documented sharing notification.

[Exam Trap] Uploading the revised document while keeping the superseded version, sometimes with a note saying which is current
Nothing tells Claude which version governs, so outputs can cite either. A working Project needs one current version and the old one removed; completeness belongs in the archive, not the knowledge base.
[Exam Trap] Adding an instruction telling Claude to prefer the newer document
This patches the instructions to compensate for a knowledge base that should simply be curated. The superseded document should not stay in a working Project, and the patch itself becomes one more stale rule to maintain.
[Exam Trap] Assuming the system will tell colleagues the configuration changed
The only documented notification is the email when a project is first shared. None is documented for later edits to knowledge or instructions, so tell colleagues yourself.

A bird observatory trust runs a Project that the bookings secretary and two other committee members use for overnight-stay booking correspondence. The booking terms were revised in March. Letters have started quoting the old cancellation notice period, and the secretary finds both versions of the terms in the project knowledge. The trust intends to keep the Project as its booking workspace. What should she do?
Option ARemove the superseded terms, check the instructions for any rule written for the old wording, and tell the other two committee members what changed and when
Option BStop using the Project for booking letters and have each member attach the current terms to every new chat instead

Option CUpload the March version of the terms again and add a line to the custom instructions telling Claude to prefer the newer document wherever the two versions disagree
Option DAdd a note file to the knowledge base stating that the March version is current, and keep both versions of the terms so the Project holds a complete record of how they have changed
[Check Answer]

Two questions decide whether a task goes to Claude. Fit asks whether Claude would do the work well: the right shape, the right volume, output someone can check. Domain 4 covers fit. Appropriateness asks whether the task should be delegated to Claude at all. It looks at different evidence: the stakes, the authority the work requires, and who is accountable for the outcome. A task can be a perfect practical fit and still be work that only a qualified human should do.

This lesson uses one made-up example throughout: a bike shop. Its owner has two jobs to do. One is a long series of customer reviews to summarise into themes. The other is a stack of applications for a mechanic's job, to score so that the owner can pick the person to hire. Scoring the applications is an excellent practical fit: structured, voluminous, checkable. It can still be inappropriate, because of what the scoring decides and who cannot challenge it. The wrong answer that appears often bases its reasoning on quality: Claude would do the task quickly and well, so it must be fine to delegate. The quality of the output does not decide whether the task is appropriate.
Four recognisable categories make a use inappropriate.

The first is work that needs professional authority: legal, medical, financial and safeguarding judgements. A qualified person must make these and be accountable for them. Claude can help someone prepare, summarise or understand. Claude cannot be the source of the advice. At the bike shop, medical advice for an injured customer must come from a qualified person. The Usage Policy names the settings where this category applies most. Its High-risk Areas include legal and medical advice, finance, credit, insurance, housing, employment, education and healthcare access. In these areas a qualified person must review Claude's recommendation before it is given as advice or used to make a decision. The policy also states: "The qualified person remains responsible for the accuracy and appropriateness of what is delivered or decided." The policy excludes wellness content, such as education on sleep, stress, nutrition or exercise.

The second is a consequential decision about identifiable people: who gets the job, the award, the sanction, the visit. Poor output is not the reason. Nobody is accountable for the decision, and the person affected cannot challenge it. The scoring of the mechanic applications belongs in this category.
The third is fabrication presented as real: invented quotes, testimonials, case studies or evidence, such as customer testimonials the shop writes itself. Plausibility makes fabrication worse, because a convincing invention is easier to believe. The Usage Policy's prohibitions on misinformation and deceptive practices are the basis of this category.
The fourth is anything the Usage Policy or the organisation's own policy prohibits. Objective 6.3 covers this category.

One test decides whether a task is appropriate. Picture a capable, well-meaning colleague who has:
no professional qualification in the area
no access to the person's history
no accountability for the outcome
Would you accept this piece of work from them? The test changes an abstract question about appropriateness into an ordinary judgement about delegation. Every professional already makes that judgement. The review summary passes: the same colleague could write it, and the owner would check it. The mechanic scoring fails on all three grounds at once. Anthropic's AI Fluency framework names this skill Delegation.

The broad range of appropriate uses matters as much as the four categories. Official documentation describes a deliberately broad range of appropriate uses: writing across formats, summarising long documents, brainstorming, analysing images and data, translating. Drafting, reformatting, analysing material you hold, and preparing someone to make a decision are all appropriate. The inappropriate categories are narrow and specific. If you treat everything near them as forbidden, you abandon work that a simple safeguard would enable. The owner can still ask Claude to summarise each application, then read the applications and choose.

This objective asks a different question from the rest of the certification. Candidates who come to it from Domain 4 reliably answer the wrong question. The substitution test covers everything the exam asks. The exam also marks over-caution as wrong: the right answer almost always makes the work possible within the rules.
What to notice in the exam

Adding review to an inappropriate delegation does not repair it. Suppose a manager checks the output of a consequential decision about identifiable people. The check restores neither accountability for the judgement nor the affected person's ability to challenge it. When the owner reads every applicant's score, neither of those two things changes. Exam options that offer review as the fix test exactly this point.

The Usage Policy's review rule answers a different question. It applies where a use in a High-risk Area proceeds. For that case, the policy states this requirement: "A qualified person must meaningfully review a High-risk AI Recommendation, with the authority to change or modify it, before it is delivered as advice". There, review is a mandatory control, and objective 2.4 teaches it as the standard. Review cannot convert a decision that should not have been delegated into one that should. Ask whether the delegation is appropriate first. Only then does the review requirement apply.

The AI Fluency framework lists the four Ds as module names and does not define them. Reading Delegation as "deciding what to hand to AI and what to keep" is our own interpretation. The Help Center's use-case article lists what Claude is for and contains no prohibitions. The inappropriate categories are based on the Usage Policy and the exam guide.

[Exam Trap] Adding a human reviewer to an inappropriate delegation and treating that as the fix
Adding review to an inappropriate delegation does not repair it. A reviewer who approves a decision made elsewhere restores neither the judgement nor a reasoned answer to the affected person's appeal. Keep the decision with an accountable person.
[Exam Trap] Accepting the argument that a use is fine because the results stay inside the organisation
Keeping an output in-house restores neither accountability for the decision it contains nor the affected person's ability to challenge it. Keep the decision with a named, accountable person.
[Exam Trap] Declining both halves of a mixed proposal

Declining everything looks cautious but loses help Claude can appropriately give. When a proposal mixes appropriate and inappropriate work, keep the appropriate half and decline only the inappropriate one.

A children's centre manager is asked to use Claude on the annual family survey. Two proposals arrive together: summarise three hundred free-text responses into themes for the service review, and score individual families' responses to flag which should receive a home visit. The service review needs the themes. Centre policy allows Claude on the survey text and bars any tool from scoring families for home visits. What should the manager do?
Option ASummarise the responses into themes once identifying details are removed, and keep the home-visit flagging with the qualified staff of the centre
Option BRun the scoring as proposed, and have the deputy manager review every flagged family before any visit, so a person stays involved

Option CDecline both proposals, since family survey material is too sensitive for any AI tool to touch
Option DRun both pieces of work, since the survey data never leaves the centre and the families consented to its use for service planning when they completed the survey
[Check Answer]

Sensitive material is anything that an organisation should not give to an outside service without a decision. It may be personal data, or it may be material that is sensitive because of who owns it or what was promised about it. A safeguard changes what leaves the organisation. The ladder is four safeguards in a fixed order. A placebo is a step that acts only after the material leaves the organisation.

This lesson uses one made-up example throughout: a day nursery. Its manager wants Claude to explain why fee arrears rose this term. Her spreadsheet holds each child's name, date of birth, address and allergy notes, and parents' account numbers and payments. If she uploads the spreadsheet unchanged, everything in it leaves the nursery. If she refuses, the arrears stay unexplained. The answer is between these two extremes: a safeguard that lets the work proceed within policy.

The obvious list is names, addresses, dates of birth, reference and account numbers, health information, financial details, and anything about children. People miss the categories about ownership and promises:
information held under a duty of confidence
commercially confidential figures
third-party material governed by a contract that says how it may be handled
A supplier's pricing schedule has no personal data. It can still be the most restricted document on the desk, because a contract may govern it. The price list from the nursery's food supplier is an example.

Anthropic's Usage Policy counts confidential or proprietary data as private information. It also counts non-public contact details and health data as private information. Under the policy, private information is not to be misused or accessed without permission. The policy also prohibits violating privacy rights as defined by applicable privacy laws, such as sharing personal information without consent.
Anthropic's protections article describes encryption in transit and at rest. It also says that Anthropic bars employee access by default. These measures protect the data that Anthropic holds. They do not replace your organisation's own decision about what may leave the organisation.

Each safeguard on the ladder preserves more of the work than the safeguard below it. So use the lowest safeguard that works.
Remove. Most analysis does not need the names. Remove the identifiers and proceed today. The arrears question needs payment patterns, so the manager removes the children's names and addresses.
Anonymise or aggregate. Use cohorts (groups of people) instead of individuals, and use ranges instead of exact figures. The nursery can group families by room and show arrears as ranges.
Use an authorised route. Move the work to a sanctioned workspace, which is the Claude workspace that your organisation provides, under an agreement that covers this class of material.

Seek authorisation. Ask whoever owns the data or the policy. Seeking authorisation is an action, not a refusal.
Abandonment is at the bottom. Anonymisation lets the analysis proceed, so abandoning the analysis gains nothing.

The policy control is about what leaves the organisation. The material leaves at upload, and a later step cannot undo the upload. Every placebo fails for this reason. The placebos are telling Claude to forget the material, declaring the upload confidential, adding a confidentiality line to the prompt, or deleting the conversation. If the nursery manager uploads the full spreadsheet and then asks Claude not to retain it, the details have still left the nursery. Nothing that is typed into the chat can retroactively govern what was uploaded. The safeguard happens before the upload or not at all.

Two current Anthropic privacy articles share the exact title "Is my data used for model training?". One article covers consumer products, and the other covers commercial products. The two articles give different answers. By default, Anthropic does not use inputs or outputs from its commercial products, such as Claude for Work, to train its models. Data handling depends on the plan, and the details have changed over the history of the documents. So ask three questions rather than memorise today's answer. Which product am I on? What does its documentation say today? What does my organisation's agreement add? The nursery manager asks these questions first. Objective 6.3 covers what follows from the answers.

In the guide's sample question for this domain, a project manager wants to upload a spreadsheet of customer names and account numbers. The right answer neither uploads the spreadsheet as it is nor abandons the analysis. It anonymises the spreadsheet so the work can proceed within policy. This pattern shows the whole objective in one example: a safeguard that enables the work, between two wrong extremes. The exam tests the order of the ladder. Abandonment is almost never the right answer, because the guide's rationale says anonymisation enables the analysis. It also says instructing the model not to retain data does not satisfy the policy control.
What to notice in the exam

Any option whose safeguard acts after the upload is wrong. No placebo is ever the right answer. The right answer changes what is uploaded, not what happens afterwards.
Deletion and retention details change often. The Domain 6 quick reference has the current, dated figures.

[Exam Trap] Treating a confidentiality instruction or later deletion as the safeguard
The exam guide says instructing the model not to retain data does not satisfy the policy control. The disclosure happens at upload, so a later instruction or deletion cannot undo it. Remove or anonymise the identifiers before uploading.
[Exam Trap] Escalating up the ladder when removal is enough
Moving the work to a sanctioned workspace or seeking authorisation looks diligent, but when simple removal of the identifiers lets the work proceed today, the higher rungs cost time for no protective gain. Use the lowest safeguard that works.
[Exam Trap] Approving a document for upload because it contains no names

Sensitivity is not only personal identifiers. Duty of confidence, commercial confidentiality and third-party contractual restrictions apply even when no one is named. Check whose material it is and what the agreement allows, then leave it out or ask the owner.
[Exam Trap] Dropping the analysis because personal data is involved
Abandoning the task is unnecessary when anonymisation enables it. Removing the identifiers lets the analysis proceed within policy, so abandoning the task loses a legitimate insight and gains nothing. Strip or anonymise first, then run it.

A minibus driver training scheme's coordinator wants to use Claude to understand why pass rates dropped this year. The trainee records contain names, licence numbers, dates of birth and medical fitness declarations. The scheme's data policy allows personal or health details into an AI tool only where the task cannot be done without them. What is the most appropriate way to proceed?
Option AStrip the identifiers and medical declarations from the records, then analyse pass rates by cohort, instructor and course date
Option BUpload the records as they stand, since the analysis is an internal review and the results will stay inside the scheme

Option CConclude that trainee records are too sensitive to give to Claude at all and compile this year on paper instead
Option DUpload the records with a confidentiality instruction in the prompt, then delete the conversation once the analysis is done
[Check Answer]

The sanctioned workspace is the Claude workspace that your organisation provides. A personal account is an account that an individual holds for themselves. Shadow AI is work material in an AI tool that the organisation does not provide. The rule is short: use the workspace that your organisation provides. The rule sounds like etiquette. It has real reasons behind it. Understanding what the rule is based on lets you answer any version of the question without memorising a table.

This lesson uses one made-up example throughout: a minicab firm that provides Claude to its office staff. A new dispatcher's access has not arrived, and a hotel contract is due on Friday. She pastes the contract and the complaints log into her personal Claude account because it is quicker. The bookings manager discovers this.

h: Why the Sanctioned Workspace Is Substance
t: When an organisation provides Claude, the arrangement governs how Anthropic handles the organisation's data. The organisation decides what happens to its data. Anthropic handles the data only on the organisation's instructions. In the Privacy Center's terms, the customer is Controller of the data that its users submit. Anthropic is Processor on the customer's behalf. The commercial training article states that by default Anthropic will not use inputs or outputs from commercial products to train its models. Administrators control the workspace's settings. On the Enterprise plan, the organisation sets custom retention timelines for its data. Users still delete their own chats from their visible history. The organisation controls the workspace's retention, but it does not control the deletion action. The agreement, the administration and the data handling all apply to the sanctioned workspace. The rule protects these three things. In the firm's workspace, the firm's agreement would cover the contract.

The individual's own consumer relationship with Anthropic governs a personal account. The individual's own settings decide whether Anthropic uses the chats for model improvement. Consumer deletion and retention rules apply. The employer does not administer, see or govern any of it. The problem is not carelessness. The organisation's agreement and controls do not apply to the account. The dispatcher's own agreement now covers the hotel contract, not the firm's agreement. A paid personal plan with careful settings would change nothing, because the question is whose agreement governs the data.

h: The Shadow-AI Response Has Two Halves
t: The response to a colleague's workaround has two halves. First, do not copy the workaround, however urgent the deadline is. Second, report the workaround to whoever owns the policy or the data. The disclosure has already happened, and someone with the authority to handle it needs to know. An unreported workaround also continues. The colleague's underlying problem is real: access has not arrived for work that is due. Only the organisation can fix this problem. When you report the workaround, the organisation learns that its access process is too slow. So reporting is not an accusation against a colleague. The bookings manager keeps her own work in the workspace. She tells the policy's owner about the disclosure and the late access. Asking the dispatcher to delete her chats or close her account does not undo the disclosure, because the contract has already left the firm.

When a policy is silent on a question, the question has not been answered. The professional action is to ask the policy's owner. This is the escalation that objective 6.2 teaches. It is an action, not a refusal. If the firm's policy says nothing about pasting complaints into Claude, the bookings manager asks the policy's owner first. The basic working habits are plain, and the exam can test them:
know which account and plan you work in
know who administers it
follow the rules for what may be uploaded
know how to report a problem
When policy conflicts with convenience, the policy takes priority. When the policy is genuinely wrong or too slow, ask its owner to change it rather than bypass it.

The scenario that appears often in the exam describes a colleague who uses a personal account for work material. The colleague does this because it is quicker or their access has not arrived. Candidates who treat the rule as etiquette lose marks to wrong options that are based on good intentions. The right answer does both halves, and candidates reliably miss the second half. Wrong options offer the first half alone, or deleting chats and closing the account as a remedy, or a paid personal plan with careful settings. The most common wrong option treats anything that the policy does not mention as allowed.
Boundary discipline

Objective 6.2 covers whether material may be uploaded at all. Domain 4 covers how to design a process. In this objective, you escalate to whoever owns the policy or the data, never to a technical specialist.
Anthropic publishes no guidance on what an organisational AI policy should contain. This objective is based on the exam guide's wording and on the documented product differences that underlie the sanctioned workspace.

[Exam Trap] Fixing only half of the shadow-AI situation
Declining to copy the workaround while saying nothing leaves the disclosure unknown and the access gap unfixed, so the workaround continues. The right answer does both halves: stop the practice and raise it with whoever owns the policy or the data.
[Exam Trap] Offering deletion as remediation for material already disclosed
Deleting conversations or closing the account is a step taken after the disclosure: the material has already left the organisation, and nobody with authority knows about it or the access gap. Stop the workaround and report both to whoever owns the policy or the data.
[Exam Trap] Treating policy silence as permission

A policy that does not mention something has not answered the question. Assuming permission converts a gap in a document into an unauthorised disclosure; the right move is asking the policy owner, which is an action, not a refusal.

The operations lead at a recycling social enterprise discovers that a colleague has been pasting the local authority contract and staff shift records into a personal free Claude account at home, because the organisation's licences have not been issued yet and the work is due. The enterprise's data rules keep its material out of personal accounts on any plan, and any slip must be reported. What should the operations lead do?
Option AAsk the colleague to delete the conversations and her account history, and confirm that the contract and the shift records are no longer held anywhere outside the organisation
Option BLet it continue until the licences arrive, since the colleague is careful about what she pastes and the work genuinely cannot wait

Option CMove the work onto his own personal account instead, since he pays for a plan with stricter data settings, closer to what the organisation will provide
Option DStop the personal-account work now, and tell whoever owns the policy about the disclosure and the licence delay so both get dealt with
[Check Answer]

Accountability means being responsible for work when the work goes wrong. Disclosure means telling people that AI helped to make the work. A stakeholder is anyone whom the work affects. Domain 2 asks whether an output is correct. This objective asks who owns the output, who deserved to know how it was made, and whom the output describes. Unlike most objectives in this domain, this objective has little documentation.
This lesson uses one made-up example throughout: a family-run takeaway that uses Claude for its newsletter, its website order chat and the weekly specials. The head cook used to write the weekly specials.

The person whose name is on the work owns it: the email's sender, the report's publisher, the letter's signer. Saying that Claude drafted the work describes the production method. It is like saying that an assistant typed the work. The statement moves no responsibility. The Usage Policy includes this rule in its high-risk requirements. The policy names High-risk Areas, such as legal or medical advice. When Claude's output becomes advice or a decision in one of these areas, a qualified person must "remain accountable for what is delivered or decided". The AI Fluency framework calls the same duty Diligence.

If the newsletter prints a wrong price under the owner's name, the owner owes the correction. Blaming Claude, or whoever configured the Project, only explains how the error happened. Under pressure, that blame is tempting, so practise the rule until you apply it automatically.

The Usage Policy sets one categorical rule. Consumer-facing chatbots and external-facing AI agents must tell users that they are interacting with AI rather than a human. This disclosure must happen at a minimum at the beginning of each chat session or in the product interface. The takeaway's order chat can open each conversation by saying that it is AI, or it can show a label in the chat window. A line in a privacy notice elsewhere on the site does neither of these things.
For everything else, disclosure depends on proportion, and both extremes are wrong. Nobody declares AI assistance on a routine internal email, such as the staff rota. Declaring everything is over-caution. Disclosure is owed when:

the reader's trust depends on who did the thinking or the judging: assessed work, a professional opinion
a claim of authorship would be false
a policy or client agreement requires it

The test is what the reader relies on. If the reader relies on the information, disclosure adds little. If the reader relies on the fact that you did the thinking, disclosure is owed. A personal message such as condolence, or thanks meant as your own feeling, is different. The reader of such a message relies on the feeling being your own. A disclosure note cannot restore that, so you write the message yourself. An organisation's routine thank-you letters are ordinary drafting work. The newsletter's prices need no note. The owner writes the thank-you card for a retiring driver without Claude.

h: Fairness Is a Different Review from Accuracy
t: An output can pass every accuracy check and still be unfair. Descriptions of groups, communities, applicants or service users can repeat assumptions that the facts never required. Suppose that the newsletter's delivery section presents one estate as a problem, a village as declining and older customers as resistant to change. Every delivery time is correct, yet the people that the section describes still see the unfairness at once. Checking the numbers misses the unfairness, because the unfairness is in how the section presents people. This unfairness needs a different reviewer: someone who knows those customers and reads for how the section describes them. The Usage Policy also prohibits using Claude to critique anyone's body shape or size. The policy treats such critique as promoting unhealthy body image.

h: Fairness Is a Different Review from Accuracy
t: Domain 2 covers spotting bias as an evaluation skill. This objective covers the responsibility half: whose job it is to catch unfairness in work about people before publishing. It also covers what the publisher owes when unfairness is published.

The stakeholder that most candidates never consider is the person whose work changes. When Claude starts to do part of a process, the colleagues who do that work need to know what changed and why. When colleagues discover that a shared task was automated without notice, that discovery damages the trust that disclosure protects. So the owner tells the head cook before Claude's first specials board is displayed. Using Claude to produce a colleague's contribution without telling them is an ethical question of honesty between colleagues, not a question of output quality. Examples are appraisal comments that the colleague was meant to write and a section that the colleague was meant to own.

Questions ask who owns an output, who should have known, who is described, or whose work changed. The right answer keeps accountability with the person named on the work. Wrong options spread accountability onto the tool or the Project's configurer, or offer a general rule to declare everything, which is over-caution.
What to notice in the exam
An option whose main content is checking, cross-referencing or validating belongs to a Domain 2 objective. The right answer for objective 6.4 is always about ownership, disclosure, fairness or colleagues.

This lesson extends the Usage Policy's high-risk accountability rule to everyday workplace outputs. This extension is the exam guide's objective, interpreted through ordinary professional practice. The same two grounds support the disclosure framework beyond the chatbot rule. They also support the section on colleagues. No first-party document covers either of these.

[Exam Trap] Transferring accountability to the tool or its configurer
Explaining that Claude produced the figure, or that someone else set up the Project, describes how the error was made, not who owes the correction. Responsibility attaches to the name on the work, so the author corrects the figure and fixes the check.
[Exam Trap] Using disclosure to avoid blame or as a rule for every output
An AI-assistance note added to soften ownership of an error misuses disclosure, and declaring assistance on every routine output is over-caution that drowns the cases where it genuinely matters. Disclosure is about what the audience is relying on, not a ritual or a deflection.

[Exam Trap] Signing off work about people once the figures are confirmed as correct
Fairness failures survive accuracy checks by definition. The characterisation review is a separate pass by someone who knows the people described, and an option that stops at verified figures has answered the accuracy question while the ethical one is still open.

The clerk of an almshouse charity publishes the annual report to residents and donors, largely drafted by Claude from the charity's own maintenance and occupancy records. A resident spots that the report overstates how quickly repairs were completed last year, and asks the clerk who wrote it. What is the professional response?
Option AAmend the figure quietly in the online copy so the record is accurate without drawing further attention to the mistake
Option BAdd a note to the report disclosing that AI was used in the drafting, so readers can weigh the figures accordingly
Option CExplain that the figure came from an AI-assisted draft, so the error is a software fault the charity will raise with the provider of the tool

Option DOwn the error as the author of the report, issue the correction to residents and donors, and fix the checking step that let it through
[Check Answer]

A poor output is a response that fails to give what the request needed. To diagnose a poor output, you name why a reasonable-looking request produced it, before you change anything. A Project's configuration is its instructions and knowledge.
This lesson uses one made-up example throughout: an independent bookshop. Its owner keeps a Project for the weekly new-titles newsletter. The owner asks for one-off shelf cards in ordinary chats.

The most useful diagnostic test is one question: did the problem happen once, or does it happen every time? A bland summary from one request that gave too little information is a prompt problem. A better brief fixes it. The same wrong tone, format or assumption in every output from the same Project is a configuration problem. The sign to look for is the word every. The Project's instructions or knowledge produce the defect, so correct the configuration once. Correcting each output by hand instead repeats the same cost forever.
One bland shelf card needs a better brief. A stiff tone in every newsletter needs one fix in the Project's instructions.

h: A Cause List You Can Run in a Minute
t:
Six causes cover nearly everything:
context starvation: a request without the context it needs
instruction overload: a request with too many requirements
a configuration defect
a degraded conversation
stale or superseded material
a feature or setting mismatch
Context starvation is by far the most common cause. A request with no audience, no purpose and no source material can only produce generic output, because Claude cannot guess what was withheld. The Help Center advises giving as much context as possible, as if instructing someone with no background knowledge of the task. Supply what was missing. Asking more forcefully supplies nothing. The shelf card needed its audience, its purpose and the book's blurb.

h: A Cause List You Can Run in a Minute
t: Instruction overload comes next. A request with a dozen requirements loses some of them. The documented remedy is structural: split complex requests into substeps, and group and prioritise the requirements so the important ones cannot be missed. Re-sending the same list with the missed items in capitals supplies nothing new. The owner splits and prioritises a newsletter brief that repeatedly loses the opening hours.

h: When the Conversation Itself Is the Problem
t: A long chat accumulates superseded drafts, corrections that were later contradicted, and unrelated topics. Claude has to work with all of it. The chat eventually reaches its length limit. Longer conversations that trigger automatic context management also consume more of your usage limit. The documented advice is to split the content into parts, summarise the important sections, or start a new conversation. Projects handle large recurring material through retrieval. To fix a degraded chat, start a new conversation that contains a verified summary of what still matters. A chat that holds three newsletter drafts restarts from a summary.

The Help Center's troubleshooting articles name this objective's symptoms. Incorrect or misleading responses include fabricated quotes that look right. Claude is not a singular source of truth. So scrutinise high-stakes claims and review cited sources, such as a newsletter's author quote. Hallucinated capability means links that look as if they work but fail, or a claim that Claude has sent an email. Claude has no access to email or to any software that is not explicitly integrated. The diagnosis is hallucinated capability, not a delivery problem to investigate.

A response that is too brief is a prompting problem, so revise the prompt. Give Claude the previous prompt and response so that it continues from the point where it stopped. Error messages are not quality defects. A capacity notice means wait and retry. A length-limit message means split the content into parts, summarise it or start a new conversation. Half of the diagnosis is recognising which of these the symptom is, because each has a different fix.

The favourite trap in this domain is to choose the most capable model or a higher effort setting because the output was disappointing. A vague brief fails with every model, because the missing context is missing for every model. Escalation produces the same generic answer, more thoroughly and at more cost, and the shelf card stays bland. Changing a feature or setting is legitimate when the task needs depth or current outside information. For depth, use the effort and extended thinking settings. For current outside information, use web search or Research. Use these features and settings only after the brief is sound.

Every question in this domain starts after something has gone wrong. Domain 1 covers how to write a good request. This domain covers how to diagnose a poor output. Domain 5 covers how to change a configuration. This domain covers how to recognise that a configuration needs a change. Candidates lose these marks when they choose a fix before they name a cause.
[Key Concept] Classify the symptom before you read the options. Did it happen once or every time, and which named failure mode is it? The right answer fixes the cause. At least one wrong option treats the symptom, usually by rewriting a prompt that was never the problem.

h: What the Sources Do Not Say
t: No official source says long chats get slower or that Claude confuses topics. The case for starting a new conversation is based on what is documented.

[Exam Trap] Rewriting today’s prompt when every output has the same defect
A defect appearing in every output of the same kind comes from the setup, so the fix belongs in the Project’s instructions or knowledge once. Rewriting individual prompts, or hand-correcting each output, repeats the same cost forever and leaves the cause in place.
[Exam Trap] Escalating to a more capable model or higher effort as the first response to a disappointing output
If the request never named its audience or attached its material, escalation returns the same generic answer more slowly and at more cost. Diagnose first: a brief without enough context is fixed by supplying context, and no model can guess what was withheld.

[Exam Trap] Treating an error message as a quality defect and rewording the prompt
Capacity and length-limit messages have documented responses: retry after a short wait, or split the content into parts, summarise it and start a fresh conversation. Rewording the request does not address what the message is about.
[Exam Trap] Investigating the delivery of an email Claude claims to have sent in a chat with no email integration
Without an integration, Claude has no email access, so a claimed send is fabricated capability, not a delivery failure. Checking outboxes or asking Claude to resend treats a send that never happened as real. Deliver the content yourself.

The administrator of a small art gallery drafts loan-request letters to lenders inside a correspondence Project. For two months, every letter has come out in American spelling, and she has corrected each one by hand before posting. A more capable model gave the same spelling. She wants to stop the hand corrections and keep drafting inside the Project. What is the most appropriate next step?
Option AKeep correcting each letter by hand before it is posted, since the fix only takes a few minutes each time, and the letters are otherwise exactly what she wants to send
Option BReview the Project’s instructions and knowledge for what produces the defect, and state the spelling standard there once

Option CSwitch the Project to a more capable model so the letters come out in the right spelling first time, with no hand correction
Option DDraft future letters in fresh conversations outside the Project so its settings cannot influence the spelling of the finished text
[Check Answer]

An adjustment round means changing a request, running it again and judging the output. Objective 1.3 taught what good feedback sounds like inside a conversation. This objective covers the discipline around that feedback. A systematic round gives you more than a different result. It gives you knowledge that you can reuse tomorrow and explain to a colleague. A systematic round needs three parts. You change one thing at a time. You hold the test input fixed. You judge the result against a criterion that you state before you look.
This lesson uses one made-up example throughout: a carpet shop. It has Claude draft the quote letter that the shop sends after each measuring visit. Customers continue to phone the shop to ask for the total.

h: Change One Thing at a Time
t: One change at a time shows what fixed the output. Suppose the owner changes only the audience line and the letter improves. Then the audience line was the problem, and that lesson applies to every similar task. Suppose she changes the wording, the model and the attached example at once. The letter improves, and nobody knows which of the three worked. Tomorrow, when she does the same kind of task, she knows no more than before. A bundled change, which changes several things at once, looks efficient until you need a second good result. Anthropic's Help Center says that an effective prompt contains as much context as possible. About adjustment, the Help Center gives no advice beyond giving Claude feedback, clarifications and rewrite requests. The one-variable discipline, one change at a time, is ordinary professional method.

A new prompt that you try on a new document tells you nothing, because two things changed. A better result may only mean an easier input. When you hold the test input fixed (the same course, report or source file), the comparison between rounds is meaningful. For the owner, the test input is one customer's measuring notes. She uses these notes in every round. When you edit an earlier message, the edit creates a different version of the chat. That version has its own artifacts. Each round can start from the same input, and you can compare its result with the round before.

h: State the Criterion Before You Look
t: "Better" is not a criterion. "A customer can find the total price in five seconds" is a criterion. Stating the criterion in advance stops your judgement from drifting towards whatever the new draft happens to do well. That drift is how you accept a round that fixed nothing. A stated criterion also makes other people's reactions usable. A returned draft and a criterion together identify which requirement failed. "The manager didn't like it" identifies nothing.

h: Feedback Arrives from Readers, Not Just the Text
t: The results that matter often come from outside the conversation. A colleague says the tone is wrong. A manager returns a draft. A reader asks the same clarifying question three times. These reactions usually show what the output lacks more precisely than you do when you re-read the text yourself. The customers who phone about the total are such a result. When you treat these results as inputs to the next round, not as noise, you can iterate on whether the output works. When you ignore them, you iterate on how the output looks.

Adjustment assumes that the approach is right and that the execution is wrong. When several well-aimed rounds have not changed the output, that assumption has failed. The task may need different source material, a feature such as web search or Research, or a different setting. The task may be work that you should not give to Claude at all. The third failed adjustment is a signal to return to the cause list in 7.1 and diagnose the cause again. A fourth round of slightly different words tests the same failed assumption. If customers still phone after the owner's third round, she stops rewording.

The exam has questions on each of the three parts. The exam presents the bundled change as decisiveness.
Where this method comes from
No Anthropic article teaches one-variable adjustment. The Help Center's advice ends at giving Claude feedback and asking for rewrites. Branching a chat only gives you versions to compare. This lesson's discipline is based on the wording of the exam guide's objective and on ordinary professional practice.

[Exam Trap] Changing several things at once and calling it decisive
Changing the wording, the model and the example in one round leaves nobody knowing which change worked, so the improvement cannot be attributed or repeated. Change one thing at a time and keep the rest fixed.
[Exam Trap] A fourth round of rewording after three aimed rounds changed nothing
Several well-aimed rounds that changed nothing mean the approach, not the execution, is wrong. Go back to 7.1's cause list and re-diagnose: different source material, a different feature or setting, or work not to be handed over.
[Exam Trap] Testing the adjusted prompt on a different document and crediting the prompt
When the input changed too, the comparison is meaningless; the improvement may only mean the new document was easier. Round-to-round learning requires the same test input every time.

The owner of a ceramics studio drafts the joining email she sends attendees before each weekend workshop, and attendees keep saying it is too long and too formal. She has time for one adjustment round this week. Which round is set up to teach her something?
Option AAdd one line naming the reader, re-run the same workshop’s email, and judge it against a criterion set in advance: an attendee can find the start time in five seconds
Option BAsk Claude to make the email warmer and shorter, and adopt the new version if it reads better
Option CRun the unchanged prompt on a different workshop’s joining email to see whether the problem follows the prompt or that particular workshop

Option DRewrite the prompt, switch to a different model and attach a friendlier example email all in the same round, then keep whichever combination works best
[Check Answer]

Overhead is anything you type, explain or attach at the start of every similar conversation. Optimising means making your work with Claude cost less time or usage. To measure the overhead, you time it and count how often it recurs. This objective covers how you work with Claude, not the business process around it (Domain 4.2).
This lesson uses one made-up example throughout: a kitchen fitter who drafts customer quotes with Claude. Each quote conversation opens with how his business works and prices a job, plus the same price list and catalogue. Timed, that is about ten minutes, three or four times a week.

Optimising differs from fiddling because it starts from a measured number. His measured ten minutes justify moving the preamble, his repeated opening text, to a permanent place. "Quoting feels clunky" justifies nothing yet except timing it. This is the honesty rule from Domain 4.5, applied to your own workflow. Improve what you have observed, and claim no saving that you did not measure.

Within a single conversation, Claude remembers the context from earlier messages. The fitter's preamble recurs because he types it again at the start of each new quote conversation. Recurring overhead belongs somewhere it only has to exist once.

Put context and rules that stay the same, such as his pricing rules, in a Project's instructions. Anthropic describes these instructions as tailoring Claude's responses for each project. These instructions suit work that needs Claude to keep consistent context across many conversations in the same Project. Put recurring reference material, such as his price list, in Project knowledge. Project knowledge makes the Project a self-contained workspace. A request that you make in nearly the same words every week becomes a saved form. You adapt that form per use. Put preferences that apply to everything you do in the account-wide personalisation settings. There, the preferences apply to all conversations.

h: Batch Related Requests, and Name Your Files
t: Two documented methods take minutes to apply. The first method is batching. Anthropic's usage guidance says to group multiple related tasks or questions in a single message rather than splitting them across exchanges. It also says to be specific and concise, because Claude can need clarification after vague queries. The fitter asks for the quote and cover email in one message. Anthropic's article on usage and length limits adds that longer conversations which trigger automatic context management consume more of your usage limit. So long working chats are untidy and also use more of your usage limit.

h: Batch Related Requests, and Name Your Files
t: The second method is file names. In a large Project, retrieval decides which material Claude uses. Anthropic states that well-named files help Claude understand and retrieve the right information. Anthropic states this alongside two other practices: referencing documents by name and grouping related documents in the same Project. The fitter renames "pl_v3_final" to "Worktop price list". Renaming a file so a stranger could tell what it contains is a real optimisation with a documented mechanism.

h: Match the Settings to the Work
t: Running everything at one setting causes problems with both routine work and deep analysis. Higher effort produces more thorough responses but takes longer and uses more of your usage allowance. Routine reformatting at maximum effort spends usage on depth that it never uses. Deep analysis that is rushed at a low setting is too shallow for the task. A pattern of slow, over-worked responses to routine work, such as his quote reformatting, is itself the measurement. That measurement shows a mismatched setting.

Some overhead is not worth removing. A twenty-minute task the fitter does once a year does not justify a Project, a saved form or an afternoon of setup. The saving never repays the setup, and the artefact he maintains becomes out of date between uses. Recognising the optimisation that costs more than it saves is as professional as spotting the one that saves more.

Most questions depend on whether the option in front of you has a number. The exam tests whether you notice, from a symptom or a measurement, where an optimisation belongs. This includes which piece of a repeated preamble belongs at which level. Sometimes an optimisation belongs nowhere. In this domain's hardest questions, the right answer is to decide, on the numbers, not to optimise. Choosing model and effort belongs to Domain 3.3, and writing the configuration belongs to Domain 5.

[Key Concept] In 7.3 questions, look for the measurement. The right answer moves measured, recurring overhead to a place where it exists once, or declines a setup that costs more than it saves. Wrong options optimise something untimed, such as an unmeasured reorganisation, or they optimise everything indiscriminately.

[Exam Trap] Sweeping workflow changes proposed on the basis of a feeling
Without a measurement there is no baseline, no way to know whether the change helped, and no honest claim to have saved anything. Time the work first; measure before you reorganise.
[Exam Trap] Building a Project or saved form for a task done twice a year
Setup and upkeep that exceed the overhead they remove are a cost that looks like an improvement, and the artefact becomes out of date between uses. The proportion rule says leave the rare task alone.
[Exam Trap] Raising effort or switching model to speed up a workflow whose overhead is a repeated preamble

Neither effort nor a model change gives Claude context it was never given, so the preamble would still be needed. A Project’s instructions and knowledge hold it once. Higher effort also takes longer and uses more of your usage allowance.

A city farm’s development officer starts every funder conversation the same way: explaining what the farm is and which programmes it runs, then attaching the same three documents. Timed, that comes to about ten minutes, three or four times a week. Each January she also spends twenty minutes preparing the farm’s annual return for the charity regulator. She will put effort only into what her timings show is costing time, and only where the saving outweighs the set-up. What is the most appropriate optimisation?
Option ACreate a funding Project, with the standing explanation in its instructions, the three documents in its knowledge, and a saved version of her usual request to adapt

Option BRaise the effort setting for funder conversations so the drafts come back more thorough and fewer rounds are needed
Option CSet up Projects and saved request forms for every task she repeats at any interval, including the January annual return, so nothing she does regularly ever starts from a blank conversation again
Option DReorganise her whole working week around Claude first, then time the results afterwards to see how much the changes saved
[Check Answer]
